subsubtopic: DELAY IN PAYMENT OF BENEFITS-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I seek the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion under Standing Order 43 and, with your permission, to make a very brief explanation of it.
The unfortunate incident in Bathurst, New Brunswick, yesterday underlines the fact that some of the problems and delays connected with the payment of unemployment insurance benefits are still affecting a good many people. I would remind the House that the minister concerned has on several occasions emphasized his willingness that the matter be studied fully by the appropriate standing committee. Since we are all agreed, I would suggest that the House might consent to my motion being put without debate.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the subject of delays in payment of unemployment insurance benefits, the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act generally and the regulations which include holiday pay, vacation pay, severance pay and similar income in the definition of earnings be immediately referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
I suggest that the motion might be put without debate.

OFFSHORE MINERAL RIGHTS-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43 I request the unanimous leave of the House to propose a motion arising from a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. It concerns the deadlock which has been created following the failure of
the federal government to reach agreement with the provinces with respect to offshore mineral rights. The result of this impasse has been uncertainty in mineral exploration development and discontent among the provinces affected. Furthermore, the people of the poorer regions of this country, who saw some promise of economic prosperity in the potential of offshore development, now find the rigid attitude of the federal government most discouraging.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall):
That immediately upon his return from Nova Scotia the hon. Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources make a statement on motions outlining the government's position concerning the sharing of responsibilities with the provinces in the realm of offshore mineral rights and the sharing of the royalties derived therefrom.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROCEDURE RESPECTING INTRODUCTION OF PUBLIC BILLS
speechtext:
May I revert to and invoke a practice which has arisen in recent years with regard to the introduction and first reading of public bills. On today's order paper there are listed some 149 bills for introduction by private members. It was not possible for the Chair to review the provisions of each of these bills. May I therefore suggest to the House that we adopt the procedure agreed upon in several recent sessions, namely, that we proceed to the introduction and first reading of these bills so that each may be scrutinized between now and its being called for second reading in order to allow the Chair to consider whether there is any defect in any such bill with respect to the practices and usages of the House.
I suggest that by unanimous consent all the public bills listed for introduction on today's order paper be deemed to have been introduced, given first reading, ordered to be printed and to stand for second reading at the next sitting of the House, subject of course to a subsequent examination as to the regularity of each bill.

February 25, 1972
Public Bills

I therefore suggest that with unanimous consent of the House all public bills listed on today's order paper to be introduced, be deemed introduced read for the first time and ordered to be printed for second reading at the next sitting of the House, subject, of course, to subsequent study establishing whether each one is in order.

Is this agreed?

subtopic: PROCEDURE RESPECTING INTRODUCTION OF PUBLIC BILLS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I raise one question for clarification. Does the reservation that Your Honour has quite rightly put upon the viability of the introduction of any of these bills imply a declaration or adjudication only when the bills come forward for debate or is it Your Honour's intention to review the whole list and express your views at some date in the relatively near future? Otherwise it would seem to me a bill which had really been improperly introduced could acquire some degree of respectability by remaining on the order paper and, as a matter of fact, could draw comment, correspondence and what have you from the public.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROCEDURE RESPECTING INTRODUCTION OF PUBLIC BILLS
speechtext:
I agree with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Edmonton West. In due course at some later date perhaps there might be consideration by the House of the suggestion of the Chair in respect of the bills about which reservations might be expressed. For the moment this is somewhat hypothetical. Having made a preliminary study of the bills it seems that at least the first 25 or 30 are acceptable from a procedural standpoint, so there would be no immediate difficulty in this regard. However, in due course and after due notice an opportunity will be given to hon. members to indicate their views about the regularity of specific bills on which I might express reservations.
Is the procedure to which I have referred agreed to by the House.

subtopic: PROCEDURE RESPECTING INTRODUCTION OF PUBLIC BILLS
speechtext: Agreed.

February 25, 1972
Speech from the Throne

I was hoping that the new Minister of National Defence would remain so that we could examine his stewardship as Minister of Finance over a number of years.
The Speech from the Throne does not, of course, disclose anything unusual. It has been commented upon by my colleagues at considerable length. The commentators outside have been even more stringent in their criticisms of the paucity of the Speech from the Throne in respect of financing or dealing with the very difficult situations facing the country, not only economically but socially and politically. Also these are not necessarily all domestic problems but include those from abroad. I must say I found that the task of writing the Speech from the Throne had been assigned to that person on the government side, who perhaps qualified as the possessor of the most purple prose that could be used. We have never seen the like of it, and I trust will never see it again. The list of legislation, of course, which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) tabled on the conclusion of the speech is a rather mixed bag of not too many things. I am sure the more controversial of those items will see the light of day last. The new Competition Act and the changes in the labour standards, as well as a few other proposals which appear there, certainly will not come forward early in the session.
At this time we are in an election year. There is no denying it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It may be next year.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Certainly, this colours the attitude of the government and the attitude of the House in this debate. I am not critical of that because the essence of politics and partisanship is exposed. This is the arena, this is the forum, and it is sometimes, Mr. Speaker, your unenviable task to act as referee in the exchange of ideas. It is a good thing your duties do not extend to being a referee of a physical exchange between hon. members. We get comments from the exterior, sometimes by editorial writers, who cluck, cluck when there has been a verbal dispute and sometimes a certain amount of verbal disarray in the House of Commons. We get this cluck, cluck and I wonder what they do in their editorial boards and editorial conferences. This is the forum for the expression of ideas. This is where the government must put its programs to the test before the representatives of the people. There is no other place for that expression.
I have absolutely no regrets or reservations about how we conduct our affairs. Do some people think this is a board room of some giant corporation called Canada or that it is an executive body? It is not. Here, we are discussing ideas and programs. We are not making the decisions which actually put these into practice. There is approval or disapproval registered on behalf of the people of Canada. The same thing takes place in the legislatures of the provinces. I sometimes feel the harshest critics of this institution are those people who know least about it, and who know least about the actual workings of this institution as well as the men and women who compose this institution, the Members of Parliament. According to some individuals, at election time the people of Canada go through the gutters of the nation, if there are such, to gather up people. If these people are so possessed of all this knowledge and science, why are they not on the scene

offering their help here rather than back at some nameless desk or behind some microphone where they cannot be seen. They are not held responsible for their ideas or expressions.
Having said that, I now turn to the minister's speech. I am sorry he is not here. He actually misled the House the other day. I asked him a question with regard to statements he had made on behalf of the government of Canada at the ministerial conference in Banff between finance ministers. He indicated at that time that I should bide my patience because in his speech he would give us the answers. I have combed that speech. I listened to it, and I combed it in Hansard, but I found nary a word of what was said at that conference. There was nary a word of the problems that were discussed. Naturally, there were the views that were leaked out of the conference. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) asked him some questions and he indicated that later in the day he would answer them. Again, there has been a dead silence on the subject. To that extent, I charge the minister not with misleading the House but with "conning" the House into deferring or turning aside some questions which could have been very embarrassing. But that is not the way to answer. If questions are serious, and these were serious questions, they are deserving of answers.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) is not a new boy in Canada. This is his third or possibly fourth cabinet appointment. True enough, it is a new portfolio for the minister but he has participated in cabinet meetings at which the economic implications for this country have been discussed. If I know my friend, the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton, he is not a silent member of the Cabinet and should know the problems. I will say that his speech yesterday was disarmingly fresh in difference of approach. I think one of the first things he has done has been to take that stable of speech writers which previously furnished speeches to his predecessor and given them a holiday. I hope he gives them a permanent holiday because from them we had pronouncements from on high expressed with dogmatic, shall we say, certainty. My colleague from Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan) tells me, there was that dogmatic certainty of pronouncements from a Delphic oracle. They were statements which came down from the Mount of Olympus. In strange contrast, the minister yesterday admitted there were difficulties and a lot of factors which made it very difficult for a Minister of Finance to accomplish his task. The best they could do was to give intelligent forecasts. But I trust this minister will not have the feeling of his predecessor, and in some ways the Minister of State who was assigned to the Minister of Finance, in that as I say their pronouncements were made with certainty.
I remember the former Minister of Finance saying many times what would happen to the economy. Now, the Minister of Finance is saying that, unless a man is a charlatan or a fool, he will not make these hard and fast predictions. I will take the minister at his word, but in that case what does he think of his predecessors who did go make these hard and fast forecasts? What does he think of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who just a few months ago said "we have turned the corner; we have mastered inflation and we can now turn to the problem of unemployment"? This administration has no more mas-
February 25, 1972

tered inflation than they have managed to crawl to the moon on their hands and knees. The minister says we are faced with the twin problems of unemployment and inflation.
It would be interesting to know the position which the Minister of Finance took at the conference in Jasper. Did he or did he not say that there is enough stimulus in the economy to deal with unemployment this year? Is the Bank of Canada now reversing its policy about the amount of stimulus that is to go into the economy because they are afraid of inflation? Do they feel that by the time we get to the end of the year the unemployment situation will have been taken care of and that in the third and fourth quarters of this year we will start moving on an upward trend? It is certainly not indicated that we are moving on an upward trend now, it has to be sometime later. Are those factors at that time going to determine the date of the elections?
We look at the forecasts, and they say that the economy is going to go forward so much in 1972. However, this disagrees with the observations of the Bank of Tokyo which says that there is going to be a slowdown in 1972 and that recovery will be slow. From what the government has said about the performance of Japan, there must be some credence in the observations of the Japanese. They cannot approbate and reprobate.
So what do we have for the forthcoming year? I expect that the Minister of Finance will give us a budget. When will this be? Perhaps the Minister of State, who still has to enter this debate, may be able to tell us when we may expect it. I do not say he will tell us that on a certain night at 8 p.m. the budget will be delivered, but he should be able to tell us in his speech how many of the glaring errors in Bill C-259 will be corrected, those that are more obvious. They knew they were wrong when the bill was before the House but because it would have been difficult to add more amendments, and they were gunshy of amendments because of the criticisms that they had faced over the hundreds that they had put in since the introduction of Bill C-259, we will now get them this year. Is the Canadian public going to have these further inequities inflicted on our economic system Those are the things we want to hear from the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Mahoney) if and when he takes part in this debate. We will see whether we are going to get the answers to the questions that I put to the Minister of Finance the other day.
I have another question: did the Minister of Finance and his officials in Jasper advise the provinces that the federal and provincial governments should end the expansionary efforts which culminated in the October mini-budget? I ask the Minister of State: is this the position of the government of Canada today, that the proposals contained in the mini-budget of October are to be the peak of the expansionary efforts of the government of Canada, and are we now going to see provincial entrenchment as a result, or just what will this be? I ask the minister to be frank with the House. The government should come clean with the people of this country. We have already seen credibility gaps right, left and centre. We have several credibility gaps in the Solicitor General's Department, as well as in
Speech from the Throne
the Department of the Minister of National Revenue as a result of being told by the Prime Minister when we were going to get the government's policy on foreign ownership. It was going to be last June and then it was going to be in September. There was a leak in September which created some difficulties at that time. Then, it was going to come before the end of the session, and in the interval we heard that it would be soon or that it would not be long delayed. The last we heard was that it was going to be introduced around February 16. Now, there is no such indication and the whole question has been put into cold storage. This is part of the credibility gap.
There is another credibility gap that I think we should put on the record. Some weeks ago the Prime Minister took one of these quasi non-political forays into Toronto that the Prime Minister loves to take these days. There, he lectured to people about what should be the work ethic of a lot of people. He said that there were jobs available in the country if only people would get off their sternums and go and get them. It was quite a lecture. Now, I will give a reply to that. It is contained in a delightful letter, and I will ask the House for some forbearance while I read it. The letter appeared in the Victoria Daily Columnist of February 16. Perhaps the Prime Minister will not like this. This may be part of bigot land and there might be some prejudice against the Prime Minister in some of the statements made.
The letter is signed "unemployed". It reads:

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Several days after Mr. Trudeau announced via a TV interview that there was an abundance of jobs in Canada, if anyone was willing to leave the cities and not expect an enormous wage, I phoned the local Manpower Office to apply for one. I am unemployed and registered with Manpower. I informed them that I was willing to go anywhere in Canada and work at any job at all.
What more could you ask of an individual?
The first person I spoke to knew nothing about these jobs, or the Prime Minister's statement, and passed me on to another staff member. This man said that he had heard that such a statement had been made, but knew nothing about these jobs, and connected me with another who was equally at loss and could not supply me with any information. By the time I had been referred to several other clerks, all presumably of higher rank, I could see that one and all treated the PM's statement as a big joke. When I finally reached the end of the "buck-passing" line, the clerk in charge admitted to me that at the present time there were no jobs to be had anywhere in Canada through Manpower.
One week later, I again phoned, and received the same runaround, being told "if there are any of these jobs Mr. Trudeau hasn't told us where they are".
Is this a true picture of the employment situation in Canada or is the PM using the old whitewash brush? Or is Manpower just not doing its job? If so, why won't they refer willing and able people to available jobs?
Does the general public know that the policy of local Manpower is when supplying a demand for hourly paid workmen to the largest federal government employer here in this area, namely DND, is to refer ex-service men who are on pension. What chance has any young man under 40 years of age to get into an hourly pay position in say HMC Dockyard, when the openings are being filled with men already on government pension? I understand a few

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
February 25, 1972
Speech from the Throne
exceptions are being made occasionally; under what conditions I do not know.
Perhaps Mr. Trudeau should look into this situation.

Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Signed . . . ?
"Unemployed".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: An unemployed Conservative?

I don't know. After all he does not express his political views. This is an attitude that one sees reflected in other letters to the press and letters to Members of Parliament. This is not a letter written to me, it is a letter written to the public and the point is clear. That is part of the credibility gap, part of the substantiation of the motion moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander).
I want to speak briefly about two matters before I return to the economic section of my remarks, Mr. Speaker. First of all, the other day I addressed a question to the Prime Minister asking if the government had abandoned its clear undertaking to the former minister of manpower and immigration, since there was an absence of any mention in the list of legislation of amendments to the Immigration Act or the Immigration Appeals Board Act. In reply to previous questions from myself and some of my colleagues the answer of the former minister was that these amendments plus a white paper were imminent, just over the horizon. It almost became a game between myself and the hon. member for Saskatoon-Humboldt (Mr. Lang) to determine what he meant by "soon". Now, we have the disquieting rumour, and it may be much more than a rumour, that up to half a dozen senior officials of the Department of Manpower and Immigration- and I know this as a personal fact-who have been working very hard on amendments to the Immigration Act in order to bring some order to a chaotic system and whose work has been put aside for an indefinite period aux calendes grecques, are about to resign or ask for reassignment. I certainly want to know why.
Is it fair that there should be over 7,500 appeals pending before the Immigration Appeals Board? The board works hard but the maximum work load that it can carry in a year is 950 cases which is a fair number. But there is a backlog of 7,500 cases. Some of the people who presently have appeals based on a bona fide difference of opinion with the Immigration Department as to their qualifications under the points system will be old men and women, have children and grandchildren before their case is reached. In the meantime, they will be suspended in limbo if the silly program which now exists and this inaction is allowed to continue.
This problem has to be resolved. I am not advocating or implementing any philosophy, "a la Joe Sedgwick", that we are going to answer this question. The system is arbitrary, and has substituted a so-called administerial discretion by a bureaucratic discretion. Any person who dares to object to an assessment of points under such a system must face a special inquiry and be subject to a deportation order before he can get to the Immigration Appeals Board.
Shame!

There is nothing more degrading, more intimidating or more of an administrative blackjack than this requirement that an immigrant, particularly one allowed in as a visitor who has made application for immigrant status to be given, say, 45 points, and then presumes-I would guess that the immigration officials even say "dares"-to question the assessment. He must go the deportation route before he can get an adjudication on his qualification on points since the Supreme Court of Canada has decided that the Immigration Appeals Board is competent to do that. One would almost think that this pile-up of appeals is part of a calculated program by immigration officials to get at the Immigration Appeals Board, to so jam up the system that something has to be done. There is something rotten in the whole set-up.
As my last point, Mr. Speaker, if I may, I should like to speak about the RCMP.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member's time has expired but he may continue with the leave of the House.
Carry on.

I wish to thank hon. members, Mr. Speaker, and I shall not abuse the privilege. The last point I wish to make deals with a subject I have raised in this House this week, and in public last week, with regard to change in the administration policy about the designation of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police-
Hear, hear!

-on buildings, on automobiles and on boats. I grant that this was not instituted yesterday nor by the present minister. But, Mr. Speaker, it has now become focussed in the minds of the public because of some glaring examples of what the minister says is merely administrative policy.
Hear, hear!

Since when is administrative policy not to be reviewed in public? What sacrosanct bureaucrat is entitled to say it is purely administrative and therefore there is nothing to it? Mr. Speaker, the minister is not honest with the people in regard to this.
Shame!

The hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Kaplan) can go out to Saskatchewan or Alberta or Manitoba where the RCMP have a fuller profile than in central Canada. This year the province of Alberta was preparing to celebrate the 100th anniversary of the original force behind the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. We are now told that they are going to be just "police" for greater identification. What arrant nonsense! All I can say is that the Solicitor General (Mr. Goyer) should meet with the bureaucrat responsible for this decision and if it is a commissioner's decision then the commissioner should appear before the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs to explain. Why is it that ordinary citizens, without any organization behind them, signed a telegram-11,500 of them-and sent copies to the Prime Minister and myself. Why is it that I have petitions from kids, and telegrams. My colleague from Vegreville (Mr. February 25, 1972

Mazankowski) has a telegram. I am told that there are in excess of 1,500 names on it, and it comes from a town that does not count 4,000 inhabitants. Protest has arisen in New Brunswick about this matter. This is not a question involving bilingualism; it is one involving the identification of the force. When I am outside "K" Division Headquarters in Edmonton, I want to see the coat-of-arms of the RCMP without having to get out of my car and walk up to the plaque to be able to read, "Royal Canadian Mounted Police". I do not want to see just the word "Police". I want to see that it is "K" Division of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
In the town of St. Albert, where there is a detachment of either 18 or 20 Royal Canadian Mounted Police force personnel who act as municipal police and provincial police, I want, when I come to their headquarters, to see clearly the words, "Royal Canadian Mounted Police". Anybody who says that tourists or the public want to be able to identify that force with the word "Police" instead of with the initials "RCMP", is crazy, because the letters RCMP stand for one thing and one thing only, one of the best police forces in the world.
Hear, hear!

I am not trying to butter up anybody when I say that. Why identify the force just as ordinary police, and I am not in any way degrading any local police forces. Surely, we must consider the identification of the RCMP.
And the history of the force.

I hope the minister will reply, and not say something like "Oh, but this does not bother anybody very much." He was on radio last night and so was I. Of course, in the province of Quebec the RCMP show a low profile. Their duties do not bring them in regular contact with the people of the province. The same is true of Ontario. In these provinces there are efficient, competent and sizeable municipal and provincial police forces. This is not always so in the rest of Canada. In many communities of western Canada the RCMP carry out very efficiently the duties of municipal police. The crime rates in those areas show the results of their presence. So, on almost the one hundredth anniversary of the establishment of the RCMP, we come down to this: they are to be shown as Police and, in small letters, presumably underneath, they will be identified as RCMP or Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Soon they will be so identified at the bottom of the decals on the side of police cars. They will be shown as RCMP where the slush and mud can cover those letters. What we want to see today on the door of a police car is "RCMP" above the crest. That is what we want.
Some hon Members: Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, I urge the House to support the amendment moved by my colleague from Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander).

speakeroldname: Mr. Ray Perrault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset,
Speech from the Throne
may I say that congratulations are in order for the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher) and the seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Lajoie). They both acquitted themselves eloquently in the best tradition of parliamentary democracy. I think we listened with enjoyment to their remarks.
In the Speech from the Throne His Excellency stated:
Throughout, pressures for change around the world emphasized to us that the excitement and the promise of modern technological achievements become hollow and mocking to those who find in society little understanding of their hopes and little provision for their needs.
He continued:
Economic security is one of the most effective forces with which to counter social isolation. Job opportunities must be found and income uncertainties overcome if all Canadians are to share in the richness of this land.
Together with my colleagues on this side of the House and, I am sure, the majority of members in this chamber, I am in profound agreement with those words and I want to relate my remarks to them. I do so, not only because of my personal convictions, but because I am associated with a Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), a government, a department and, indeed, a minister with a deep concern for those in need and those threatened by economic insecurity.
For almost two years I have worked with a minister who has demonstrated beyond question that he cares about people and has compassion for them. If he were in the chamber he would be embarrassed to hear me utter these remarks.
He certainly would be.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
speechtext:
A great many measures which have been advanced by the minister and by this government are overwhelming evidence of the government's concern for people. The newly appointed Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mackasey), with the full support of his colleagues, has advanced social legislation of real worth. Many members of this House have supported that legislation. Within the ambit of the Department of Labour there have been such advances as equal pay for similar work, maternity leave, severance pay, provision for individual and group notice and an end to loss of employment because of the inequities of garnishee. While he was Minister of Labour, with the support of our Prime Minister and his colleagues, he introduced proposals to revise the old Industrial Relations and Disputes investigation Act. Among its several provisions is one designed to enhance the security of Canadian workers confronted by the impact of disruptive technological change.
If the minister were not incapacitated he would be speaking here today in my stead and discussing with hon. members the subject of unemployment insurance. I am pleased to tell you that he will be back soon.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
speechtext:
He wants me to express to members in all parts of the House his thanks for the letters, cards and expressions of sympathy which have come from all sides of this House.

February 25, 1972
Speech from the Throne
A few months ago, with the overwhelming support of the House, support which extended at times to assistance in evolving details of the legislation, the minister brought into being the new Unemployment Insurance Act.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
speechtext: At times, certain hon. members suggested changes and variations in the act. Hon. members associated with the committee, throughout the long hearings and the meetings that were held, attempted to construct what we hoped would be the finest program of unemployment insurance in the whole world.
And you all failed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
speechtext:
All hon. members agreed about the need for change and reform in those measures designed to provide income protection for the unemployed and those temporarily without work. Indeed, Canada and Parliament made history last year because, undoubtedly, even if one considers the difficult period of transition, the new unemployment insurance plan is the most advanced measure of its type in the whole world.
A few months ago I attended an international congress of those responsible for the administration of unemployment insurance schemes in many nations, and it was conceded that our program was the best and most comprehensive.
Then, why is it not working?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
speechtext:
Here is a measure which recognizes the new social fact that job disruption can affect anyone. For this reason, unemployment insurance is now almost universal, or has been as of January 1, with 1.2 million Canadians having been added to the scheme and I think they are pleased to participate in the new unemployment insurance plan.
Eligibility requirements for benefits have been substantially modified, with the result that it is now much easier to qualify for benefits. The benefit level itself, up to $100 a week, is related to current earnings and there is provision for automatic adjustment to this benefit level in relation to a change in average earnings. Benefit duration is related not only to recent work history but also to prevailing economic conditions. A claimant assistance program has been established whose objective is to help claimants get work by providing job search information and guidance. The object, surely, Mr. Speaker, of this plan and other allied plans must be to assist the workers of Canada to return to useful employment as quickly as possible. That is why, when appropriate, claimants are directed to agencies for job placement, counselling or financial assistance.
Here is a measure which recognizes the fact that there are three million women in Canada's work force, with vast numbers of them providing their families with the economic margin between grinding poverty and a decent level of living, women who now have the right to pregnancy benefits when their earnings are interrupted by such natural events. Here is a measure which regards Sickness on the job or off the job as an interruption of earnings, a measure which recognizes that family costs continue,

regardless of the reason a breadwinner becomes ill. These and other important features of the legislation became available on June 27 last with full operation becoming effective last January 1.
I am well aware of the fact, as is the minister, that there have been criticisms of the plan and its implementation. Indeed, members from all parts of the House have demonstrated remarkable and commendable diligence on behalf of their constituent claimants. That is the job of all of us, wherever we sit in this House, to work for our constituents and make sure they are well served by the programs available to them.
Whenever a fundamental change as vast as this is introduced, inevitably a transition period, an adjustment period, occurs. Apart from the administrative challenges and the countless procedural considerations, there is the task of education. Even today, eight weeks after universality, about 80 per cent of the calls to Unemployment Insurance offices across Canada relate to matters other than claims. The majority are from people seeking information.
Having said all this, it is interesting to note, however, that while members have made known the problems of their constituents, none have asked abandonment of the plan because the unemployment insurance reforms in Canada were long overdue. We know that unemployment is critical to the individual regardless of a man's political belief or any other consideration. Parliament can be proud of its work. The task is to make the new plan work as effectively as possible.
I assure you that the criticism of Unemployment Insurance which has been voiced over recent months has not been dismissed lightly by the minister. You know him too well. You know him as one who gets things done, especially where people with problems are concerned. As a matter of fact, he is so busy at the hospital that he may have to come back to the House early in order to get a rest. No matter how few people are deprived of their legitimate benefits, and the number involved has been very small in comparison with the total, to those people, those families, it is a considerable tragedy and this government, in fact no government, can remain complacent while such need exists.
The minister has taken action. During the recent recess the minister held discussions with interested groups and Unemployment Insurance Commission officials to determine the validity of the criticism and to determine whether changes ought to be made in the processing of claims that would more effectively deal with the needs of the unemployed. The minister announced early this year that all claims filed would be reviewed to determine if in fact there was cause for special measures. While individual delays cannot be excused or avoided, it is a fact that the vast majority of all claims filed with the commission are processed within the prescribed time. Some hon. members have asked what is the "prescribed time". The suggestion is that our concept may be different from theirs.
The new act provides a two-week waiting period before payments are made. In effect, this means that when a claim is filed a person must have had a two week gap in his earnings. Since payments under the act are made in
February 25, 1972

arrears and since a claimant must declare that he was in fact unemployed and available for work for the period of his unemployment, it stands to reason that payments are not normally made until the fourth week of unemployment.
The investigation conducted by the commission identified three main areas of claim delay. First, some claimants fail to complete their application forms accurately. I believe the claim reform is now in its sixth review. We have invited the Canadian Labour Congress and other interested bodies to suggest form modifications which will make it as simple as possible for the claimant to file his application. Second, some employers fail to provide employees with their contributions records or their separation certificates. Third, a number of errors occur in the processing of the claims. That is not denied.
The commission has undertaken an extensive effort to provide claimants with detailed information in order to assist them in understanding the procedures involved and to help them complete their forms accurately. The commission has established, in addition to its regular offices, an extensive network of service centres for the purpose of giving effective service to claimants. The commission is continuing its efforts to identify problem areas and to evolve more effective means of dealing with claims.
It can be said that in recent weeks there has been a substantial improvement in claims processing. Members will recall that last week the minister announced the results of a survey he had requested of all claims filed since December 1971. The survey revealed that a majority of claims had been delayed through a lack of vital information from either the employer or the claimant. Some 5,000 claims, less than 1 per cent of the total claim load, were discovered to have been late.
I remind hon. members that 600,000 cheques are processed every two weeks. In the month of January, there was a payout of $130 million. This is a massive program. Every effort is being made to reduce delays to that irreducible minimum. In saying all this, I do not deny that the problems of the 5,000 were very real. Understandably, they were not interested in statistical analysis. They were not interested in a debate between the Minister of Manpower and Immigration and opposition critics on the subject of statistics. I think all of us are concerned about the individual and his well being.
No one denies the right of working Canadians to receive unemployment insurance benefits when their earnings are interrupted, but I want to say a brief word about another group of workers who deserve consideration. They are the workers of the Unemployment Insurance Commission who have been confronted with the heavy burdens imposed by the transition period. They have put in many hours of overtime in recent weeks or months. They are workers in their own right-workers without a right to reply in many cases to the criticism which has been directed against them. Like all of us, they make mistakes, but they are a remarkably efficient group. I think members will agree that reported cases of delay are dealt with promptly by the commission personnel.
At times they have been criticized most unfairly by the media and some members of the House.
Speech from the Throne
I suppose it may be tempting for some to traffic in human misery.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
speechtext: But, fortunately, most of the media and the members have resisted this temptation. Most of the members have been very cooperative. On behalf of the minister, I thank them. However, there are exceptions. Was the public interest served a while back when wide publicity-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order please. Is the hon. member rising on a point of order?

Yes, Mr. Speaker. I object to the remark of people trafficking in human misery. All of us have had to do a lot of work with regard to the problem of Unemployment Insurance claims. I do not mind the parliamentary secretary defending his employees. That is probably his responsibility, but it is not right-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member will recognize that this is hardly a point of order. It is a matter of debate between the hon. member and the parliamentary secretary. Perhaps the hon. member might want to take part in the debate later.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I say that the hon. member is in that great majority of members who have attempted to make this plan work, and I am pleased to take this opportunity of so stating; but there have been other examples where the responsibility of certain statements made both inside the House and outside can be questioned.
Why don't you withdraw your remark?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
speechtext:
It may be tempting for some to criticize the plan, but I ask was the public interest served awhile back when wide publicity was accorded to a claimant who filed a claim for benefit and who complained of inexplicable delays in getting paid? It was determined that this lady had been advised within days of filing her claim that she did not have the required labour force attachment to qualify. However, the news story dealing with this case completely ignored this fact. What was even more unfair was that the article went on to describe the personal difficulties of the person, stating that she and her family were faced with unnecessary hardship as a result of commission inefficiency. I do not think that was fair.
Last Saturday a story appeared in the Globe and Mail to the effect that the computer had produced 300 blank cheques. First of all, this is not technically possible on the computer. It could occur on an ordinary piece of equipment that is still used for some payments, and this piece of equipment is called the "interpreter". After an exhaustive and costly search throughout last weekend, the commission identified the possibility that one such cheque could have been produced several weeks ago.
Then, the hon. member talks about unfair statements on my part. Let me give a specific example which should be brought to the attention of this House. A question was asked in this House on February 18 by the hon. member

February 25, 1972
Speech from the Throne
for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), who made the breathless allegation that 5,000 claims could not be processed in the commission's Montreal pay centre and had to be moved to Belleville for processing.
What are the real facts? It is a standard emergency procedure, in any pay centre and in any operation of the magnitude of the commission's, to have standby facilities in case of snow storms or other situations which could backlog the work. In fact, however, no work from the Montreal region was done at the Belleville computer centre last week or in the recent past. Yet, the member chose to make an issue of a perfectly prudent provision of administration which anyone should be happy to know is available to meet problems.
The hon. member went on national television to, in effect, tell people from coast to coast that they could not have confidence in the Unemployment Insurance Commission because of these alleged procedures. What does the hon. member want to prove? I will let him answer that question, but my advice to him is simply that if he wants to seek out so-called "informants" from within any government organization, he should at least retain reliable informants. Better still, he should check his allegations with responsible people.
Much has been said about the unemployment insurance service in Bathurst. Indeed, in recent hours there have been reports of public demonstrations there. The Bathurst office is served by a staff of 17 in recognition of the varied problems which can arise in a community of 15,000 people. The claim load in the Bathurst office is in the area of 10,000. Last week, 172 cases of alleged delay in payment were presented at the Bathurst office. To begin with, 32 of these cases were duplicates. Of the net total of 138, 22 cases involved some form of delay. Among the 22, those entitled to payment have been paid. Twenty-two out of 10,000! Not good enough, but pretty good.
Perhaps the best answer to those critics of the service in Bathurst is to be found in a report from the Moncton Times dated February 23. In part it reads as follows. The headline is "Claims Reports Blown Up-Labour Federation".
The New Brunswick Federation of Labour says the claims crisis at the Bathurst Unemployment Insurance Commission has been blown out of all proportion.
Greg Murphy, the federation's secretary-treasurer, said Tuesday that the Canadian Labour Congress in Ottawa had learned that there were not nearly as many claims outstanding as had been reported by protesters.
Mr. Murphy was commenting on a statement released by federation president Paul LePage which said that information received from meetings in Ottawa "conflicts" with reports they had received from the regional development organization known as CRAN.
The Secretary-treasurer said officers of CRAN had contacted the NBFL complaining about the claims situation and looking for financial aid to support continuing demonstrations at the Bathurst UIC office.
He said the federation refused the financial aid, but decided to have the Canadian Labour Congress in Ottawa investigate.
Mr. Speaker, some members opposite say that they are allies of the Canadian Labour Congress. There may have been a communications problem in parts of the UIC, but there is certainly one between the CLC and certain hon. members opposite. The article continued:
[Mr. Perrault.)
They found, he said, "that there weren't nearly as many claims as CRAN said there were."
"This thing has been built into a bigger thing than it actually is."
Nevertheless, he said, the CLC in co-operation with the NBFL has appointed Bill Craig, a steelworker representative in Saint John to act as a special CLC representative in the Bathurst region.
"All legitimate claims will be channeled through Mr. Craig," he said. The CLC representative would then meet with UIC officials to do what he can to straighten out the matter.
Mr. Murphy said the CLC representative would act on behalf on any person, whether labour oriented or not.
That is a constructive approach on the part of the CLC. In marked contrast to the half-truths and rumours and other kinds of tawdry and tattered reports which have been hauled into this House by certain members, the CLC, Mr. Speaker, acted with a sense of responsibility.
Today another report was brought breathlessly into this House by one of the hon. members opposite. He declared that in excess of 200 claims in New Brunswick were being delayed beyond the number of days mentioned by me earlier this day during the question period. Let me tell the hon. member that if he would get on the telephone he would determine that all these claims have now been fixed up. So, let us check our facts first, whether we are on the government or on the opposition side, before levelling criticisms against this great plan.
I repeat that when a man is unemployed it is dangerous and immoral to traffic in his human misery. And one does traffic in human misery by failing to check ones facts.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
speechtext:
If the object of the Bathurst demonstrators was to draw to the attention of the UIC and the government certain problems that were confronting one segment of the population, then they have made their point. The service at Bathurst has been measurably improved, and I would be pleased to enumerate these improvements for hon. members.
One can well understand the sense of frustration at high unemployment levels. Indeed, efforts are underway at both federal and other levels of government to increase employment and to stimulate industrial development. If I were unemployed and were living in New Brunswick, I, too, might participate in jobless parades. Indeed, I suggest any hon. member might. But I say that in choosing the Unemployment Insurance Commission as their target, I believe that as of today these Bathurst demonstrators are misguided. Their point has been made. Further demonstrations-

speechtext: May I call it one o'clock?

speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.
February 25, 1972

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier in the debate, one can understand the sense of frustration in Bathurst arising from high unemployment. Efforts are proceeding at the federal level and at other levels of government to increase employment and to stimulate industrial development. But the point has been made. Further demonstrations are self-defeating. Indeed, such demonstrations do a positive disservice to those who have a right to unemployment insurance benefits. The disruption of procedural routine in the UI office in Bathurst can only mean hardship for those who are out of work.
In recent days a number of demands have been made that the question of unemployment insurance be brought before the appropriate standing committee of the House of Commons. I would remind hon. members of the words of the minister on February 15, when he said:
I am well aware that delays which did occur in December and January and which we have now corrected have been of considerable concern to Members of Parliament. As soon as parliament reconvenes I would welcome an invitation from the chairman of the House committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration to take the initiative to have the situation reviewed by his committee. It may be that a great deal of the concern which has surrounded the situation stems from an incomplete understanding of what the claiming of unemployment insurance entails. Purely as a suggestion, therefore, I believe it would be most important that the committee should take the time to visit and study the operations of the Commission within its offices. We shall spare no effort to make sure that Members of Parliament have every opportunity to examine the operation of the claims process and to make any recommendations they see fit.
The minister has asked me to reiterate his desire to have this matter brought before the appropriate standing committee, not in order that there may be a partisan political debate but in order to determine how we can make the world's best unemployment insurance program work at its most satisfactory level of efficiency.
As hon. members know, before this matter can be considered by a standing committee the House must debate the question and must refer the matter to Committee. However, I am encouraged to learn that the standing committee will be meeting next week. Hopefully, early committee meetings will be held to discuss the question of unemployment insurance. The matter under discussion next week is, I believe, the committee's organization and procedure. Hopefully, meetings to discuss unemployment insurance will take place after the House has taken appropriate procedural action.
In recent days the suggestion has gone forth that there should be more offices established, more telephone lines, more staff and more computers. Let me give you some figures. Prior to implementation of the new act there were 65 full time offices and 67 localities where services were provided on a part-time basis of one to three days per week. There are now 119 full-time offices and 85 localities where service is provided on an itinerant basis of one to three days per week. Furthermore, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mackasey) has made quite clear that the close to 400 offices of his department will assist in every way possible in dispensing co-ordinated services with the Unemployment Insurance Commission. This process of integration is well advanced. Today, in at least 43 localities across Canada UIC offices are located in
Speech from the Throne
the same buildings as Canada Manpower Centres. While the UIC works with Members of Parliament, unions, companies, welfare groups and other organizations, the doors, the telephones and the mails of the UIC are open to all and the capacity to meet the public by all these means has been multiplied many times in the past few years.
Unlike other organizations, including most welfare agencies, which operate only on a scheduled interview basis, the UIC meets people and answers their inquiries as they come. There are approximately 1500 employees alone whose task is to answer inquiries. Last year 8 million inquiries were handled. This year, the annual rate will be about 12 million. Special attention is not accorded to Members of Parliament or the unions or the social agencies-
What about the special phones.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
speechtext:
-but to the claimants because these officers are appointed to serve people regardless of political stripe. In fact many MPs and many elected members at other levels have gone out of their way to seek out problems and it is their right to do so as representatives of the people. In this regard, the minister wants to thank the many Members of Parliament of all parties who have written to him and to the UIC thanking them for their help. The commission, as an agency dealing directly with a large public, deals with more than 6 million employees, more than 400,000 employers and more than 1.5 million individual claimants in a year. The commission has always tried to co-operate with the people's representatives as a matter of policy and service.
In summary, lest we all become confused by the great welter of statistics which has been showered down on us in recent months, I should like to outline to hon. members just what would happen to, say 100 claims filed with the Unemployment Insurance Commission today. First of all, all 100 would receive a notification of the status of their claim within two weeks. Eighty-eight would be told that their claim is in order and they would receive a cheque within a week or 10 days. Ten would be notified that payment of their claim would be postponed or disallowed for any number of reasons including participation in a labour dispute, vacation pay, severance pay, non-availability, voluntary quits, and so on. Two of these 100 would be told their claim cannot be processed for payment unless missing information is supplied or explanations are provided as to discrepancies in information supplied by claimants and their employers.
In any event, the Unemployment Insurance Commission paid out $102 million last December as compared with $60 million in December 1970, and $130 million this January as compared to $85 million last January. In both months the rate of unemployment was more this year than last. This would indicate to me that not only is someone getting paid but that the welfare savings in respect of unemployed unemployables must be substantial, totally apart from the job-creating impact of these dollars.

speechtext:

February 25, 1972
Speech from the Throne
