speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Five minutes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the members of the House for their courtesy. As I was saying, this "payout" indicates to me that not only is someone getting paid but that the welfare savings in respect of the unemployed must be substantial, totally apart from the job-creating impact this kind of money means for the economy. It is estimated, for example, that in the year 1972 welfare services across Canada will be saved $80 million as a result of this new Unemployment Insurance plan with its lower eligibility. It is no wonder that the Toronto welfare administration stated the other day that substantial savings are being realized in the greater Toronto area as a result of the new Unemployment Insurance plan.
Whenever particular cases are brought to our attention or to the attention of the commission they are investigated immediately and corrective action is taken if necessary. But again let me emphasize that in most cases many delays have been found to be outside the control of the commission staff itself.
There has been a great deal of misguided criticism of the computer system which the commission has been using for the past three years. It is hoped that further sophisticated computer technology will assist the commission to provide even more efficient computer service across this country. It is always easy to try to find a single cause of blame such as the computer. The fact is that the introduction of the computer has enabled the commission to introduce procedures which speed up the processing of claims and avoid inconveniences and difficulties for the vast majority of people. I am sure no one would want to return to the humiliating days when people had to line up every week at the unemployment insurance office in order to collect their benefits.
It must be made abundantly clear that unemployment insurance is not welfare. It is an entitlement and the claimant must prove his entitlement by meeting all the conditions of the law and by providing all the information required to make a proper decision. There will always be conditions which postpone the payment of benefits because these conditions have not been met. People must be available, capable and searching for work and they must not be the cause of their own unemployment. The law is very clear on these points and postponement of benefits due to these reasons should not be viewed as delays.
Again, it should be said that the minister has indicated that he wants these and other matters to be discussed before the committee when the committee chooses to invite him to one of its meetings. I am convinced that a great deal of concern which has surrounded this situation results from an incomplete understanding of what the payment of unemployment insurance benefits is all about. I would suggest it would be useful for the committee to take the time to visit and study the operation of the Unemployment Insurance Commission within its offices.
We are aware of the fact as well that there is some difficulty in respect of vacation pay, holiday pay and associated matters. These questions are now under detailed review by the minister and by the department.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Laniel).]
Meetings have been held with representatives of the trade unions and submissions have been received from these and other groups in respect of these aspects. Hopefully the questions of holiday pay and severence pay may be clarified in the near future.
There is clear evidence that the publicity given by the media in recent weeks is having some beneficial impact because we are finding that claimants and employers are being more careful in submitting the proper information whenever a claim is filed. I suggest that once the public at large has become more familiar with the requirements of the program fewer delays will occur. I invite any member of the House to bring to our attention any case in which they feel there has been undue delay and I undertake to ensure that every situation will be looked into promptly. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, the Canadian Unemployment Insurance program, in our view, is one of the best in the world and I am confident that most of the major questions in the program will have been resolved in the very near future.
Let us all endeavour, without partisan disputation to make certain that this program works as effectively as possible. This is in the interest of all Canadians because unemployment does not exempt anyone because of his politics, religion or ethnic background. It is a personal disaster for that person. He must be provided with income support during that time when he is without funds and we must make sure that this plan works. The hon. members on both sides who have been very helpful in an effort to make unemployment insurance work better have the thanks of the department, the government the minister and, undoubtedly, the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a certain amount of nostalgia that I rise to speak in this Throne Speech debate on February 25, 1972 since, as a great many of you know, I have more or less burned my bridges behind me. A new, young, bright candidate who is to run under the banner of the Conservative party in my riding has been nominated. So I say with a feeling of nostalgia that this may be the last Throne Speech debate in which I will have a chance to participate.
While I am on that matter, I would like to say that I appreciate the camaraderie which has existed in this chamber throughout the years. The friendships, the associations and the goodwill have always been part of the feeling that I have had for this chamber and this has been accentuated by my associations with my colleagues on both sides of the House.
When I say "Thank you" I would like to say that I bear the same feeling toward all those who have occupied the Chair in which you are sitting today, Mr. Speaker, all the members of the staff who sit at the table and all the people who have made this organization work from day to day. It has been a tremendous experience for me. My days are numbered by what we call destiny or by the Lord, but my days in the House of Commons are numbered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) of Canada. It is as simple as that.

Hear, hear!
February 25, 1972

On the occasion of the nomination meeting in my riding I was much impressed by the fact that seven outstanding Canadians presented their names for the opportunity to represent our party in that part of the world. It was also gratifying to note the tremendous interest that was created at that meeting. We had the biggest meeting that I have ever seen, probably because I was leaving and getting out of the picture. At any rate, over 900 people attended that meeting in my own village that night. It gave me a tremendous feeling of satisfaction that through the interest that was created at that meeting I was assured that the young individual who had been chosen that night was going to come to the House and sit on the same side of the House as the Conservative party. I feel that the reason the interest was created was probably that the people are beginning to realize that our leader, the Hon. Robert Stanfield, is an honest, sincere man and a great organizer who will be given the opportunity to lead this country after the next election campaign.
Hear, hear!

Having said that, I would like to join all those who, as is customary in the Speech from the Throne debate, have congratulated the mover and seconder who brought honour to themselves and to their particular areas by being chosen for this duty. Probably the one whom I know best is the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher), and I would like to say a word about the things he said in the House that day. As I remember the comments that were made about him when he was a member of the Ontario legislature, he was at that time considered to be one of the most quiet and sedate people. He spent a great deal of time criticizing the government of Ontario. I have watched him in the House and I have noticed that it is a little hard for him to sit quietly on the government benches when he feels that things are being done with which he does not entirely agree. However, the peons of praise that he heaped on the Trudeau government would appear to have all the earmarks of the preacher preaching for a call. Someone started the rumour that he may be slated for the Senate one of these days. No doubt he is one of those members who make cabinet ministers wince at caucus meetings, so probably they will be glad to get him out of the chamber and into the Senate where he might be a little quieter.
Having spent a great deal of time in my riding, which adjoins that of the hon. member for Bruce, I have the suspicion that the great flood of oratory he released upon this chamber was engendered by the criticism of the government which was heaped upon his head during the Christmas recess. If he took the course which I did of speaking to individuals and groups, he must have found it appalling that a government which had just three and a half years ago risen to such peaks of national popularity by the use of such catch phrases and charisma as the just society and participatory democracy should have engendered the oft repeated phrase which I heard during the recess, namely that Trudeau must go. I was flooded with this during the recess. One wonders how this could have happened in such a short time. Probably the Chamber of Commerce summed it up best in their brief to the government on January 31 of this year when they said the following:
Speech from the Throne
As a matter of fact, Mr. Prime Minister, during the year 1971 the chamber had over 125 substantive contacts with you, members of your cabinet and their officials, and Senate and House of Commons committees, including representations on most of the major legislative issues facing parliament last year. Despite this, I think it would be fair to say that, at the present time, there is a certain feeling of confusion and frustration on the business side with respect to business-government relations. There is a feeling among businessmen that even if they are being listened to, their views are not being understood by some government policy makers. There is a feeling that they are not getting through to those in government responsible for decision-making. There is a feeling of impatience among businessmen that their attempts to develop strong, growing enterprises are not appreciated, or sympathized with, by some responsible government representatives.
This brief was presented on January 31 of this year. Just the other day someone asked the Prime Minister in the House what the government had done to allay the confusion among the business world which started last fall. We all remember the group of businessmen who came to Ottawa in late November or early December, about the time we were discussing the tax bill. We all remember, too, how they went away shaking their heads because they were not any more knowledgeable about the tax bill when they went away than when they had come. They were disturbed and confused by the number of regulations and controls that had been presented to them. As I said, the other day the Prime Minister said that all these problems were solved by the budget in October and by the fact that the government had stabilized the dollar. He said that there is no more confusion in the business world, that it had all been straightened out. This is not true because this brief was presented on January 31 and the budget was brought down in October.
I should like to make one final quotation from this brief which substantiates what I have been saying. It refers to the tax reform and reads:
We would like to stress that, in the final result, the actual process involved in the development of the tax reform legislation created a very high degree of uncertainty and confusion among persons who must make decisions having a direct bearing on the forward thrust of the Canadian economy.
The words "confusion" and "uncertainty" are reiterated time and time again. This feeling does not only occur among businessmen. It also occurs throughout every segment of our economy. The fact is that this confusion and frustration were not only felt by the members of the business community but by the thousands of unemployed, thousands of old age citizens who find their life savings melting away under the onslaughts of our uncontrolled inflation, and by the small businessmen and farmers who could not comprehend the complexity of the capital gains tax and its effect on their personal holdings.
Is there any wonder, when one looks at this mess, that the chorus was unanimous from all quarters in my own riding that Trudeau must go? It is easily seen that the government appreciates that its stock has dropped to a very low ebb. Today one hon. member put a question to the minister in charge of Information Canada. He asked why the department was spending an extra $52 million, or some such figure, on government information services. We know that the government is disturbed about what people are thinking because everyone is being flooded with these pamphlets, such as this one entitled "Highlights for Individuals-Tax Reform and You", and "Rental

February 25, 1972
Speech from the Throne
Income and Undeveloped Land-Tax Reform and You", and "Goodwill and Similar Assets-Tax Re'form and You", and "Valuation Day-Tax Reform and You". And so it goes, Mr. Speaker. Floods of information and material come out of government offices trying to explain to the people of Canada what all this legislation means to them. But they cannot understand it; they do not know what to do and so are confused and disturbed. They feel that we must have a change.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration spoke about the situation at Bathurst, and other members have talked about the confusion at unemployment insurance offices. I have here a letter that just came yesterday from a man who has not worked since November 23. When I wrote to the minister about this on January 26 the man had not received a cent of unemployment insurance. It is interesting to note that, according to the letter from the minister's office, all of a sudden on January 24 a computer payment of $486 was made and the next day a manual payment of $437 was made.
Where is this great organization, this great unemployment insurance program that the parliamentary secretary claims is the greatest in the world? When I hear the hon. member for Bruce and the parliamentary secretary talk about programs like the unemployment insurance, the veterans' affairs and the old age pension being the greatest in the world, I wonder what the man in the moon is thinking. We will be up there one of these days. Will they be the greatest program up there, too, or on Mars? I have sat in this House for a number of years, Mr. Speaker, and I know the problems that exist from province to province and region to region. You cannot take the programs that work in other countries and expect them to work here. They talk about our programs being the best in the world but a lot of people, particularly the unemployed under 24 years of age trying to find work with no hope for the future, are not so sure that they are the best.
The Globe and Mail which carried the headline about Bathurst has another headline "35 per cent out of work in building unions-highest rate ever". I was a member of the government that inherited the tremendous unemployment problem in 1957-58. It was not created by the Conservative government but was inherited from an overbearing government that had sat for over 22 years. What did the Conservatives do about it? They brought in the winter works program. Last year in this House it was suggested that in view of the unemployment situation the Prime Minister should initiate a winter works program, but we were told that this was an outmoded approach and would not be used. Then, all of a sudden the Prime Minister saw the light. When he realized that the problem would not just go away, there was a crash program for employment and help to municipalities which was the same as the old winter works program. But the Conservative program had put a lot of carpenters, electricians and service people to work during the winter who had previously been drawing unemployment benefits. They were given jobs to help householders fix their premises. The slogan was "Why wait for Spring-Do it now" and it was successful.
Last fall an organization of people engaged in construction presented a brief to the government pointing out that the cost of a house had increased by approximately $1,000 in the last year and suggesting that removal of the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials would help reduce that increase. Nothing was done about that.
There has been a lot of talk about providing housing for people on middle and low incomes. Even if some of these people could manage to buy a home, they could never manage to get it paid off. Surely, the insurance companies and banks, even the Bank of Canada, could sit down together and find a way of reducing interest rates so that the average individual could afford to buy a house. With interest rates of 9 per cent or, 10 per cent and 15 per cent or 20 per cent on second mortgages, it is pretty difficult for the average individual to manage, even if he can get the down payment together. It means that he will carry a load for the rest of his life. There was nothing in the Speech from the Throne about help in these two areas.
Mr. Speaker, when I first participated, in a Speech from the Throne debate on December 1, 1953, I spoke about the importance of decentralizing industry. In the area I represent there are small communities which have been crying out for industry and assistance from governments for many years. They would like to get a little factory or something to provide employment for young people graduating from high school so that they would not have to leave the area. I have been calling for this for years and on December 1, 1953, I used the following quotation, which appeared at page 530 of the Hansard of that date:
We have heard it said, and we presume that it was meant seriously, that it was the desire of our great leaders to decentralize industry and to build up the smaller communities where the labour situation is easier and the living costs are less.
After the end of World War II, we lived under the threat of atomic warfare but today I think we have a greater challenge, that of pollution and destruction of our natural environment due to the urban sprawl which is causing so many problems. When the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) was in charge of housing he talked about satellite cities as did his successor. One of the reasons I have been so interested in the location of the international airport to be built some place north of Toronto is that I know it to be a slow growth area. Many communities there have lost population over the last 25 years. In a township in my riding there are 67,000 acres and only about 50 active farmers, so it could accommodate the airport. It would create incentive for all the little towns and communities and enable them to grow. I think this is a matter worthy of serious consideration and that is why I presented a motion in the House recently.
I sometimes feel that big decisions involving 50,000 or 100,000 people should not be left to the bureaucrats in the deputy minister's office to make but should be made by all members of the House. I think a committee of this House should look at the sites in question, then sit down with the people of the area to discuss the matter. That way the best interests of the people concerned and the best interests of the country will be maintained. It is the best way to consider the site of an international airport such as the one to which I am referring.

February 25, 1972

I know some will say that if the committee looks at any particular site or parcel of land, some people may assume that the government intends to establish the airport at that site, buy up land in the area and drive up land prices. Nevertheless, there are federal and provincial organizations that can take care of this sort of thing. Of course, if four different sites are looked at, for example, the committee could make its report or recommendation in camera, and that report can be forwarded to the officials of the department. I think that is the way a decision as vital as this ought to be taken. That is why, when I saw an item in the Toronto Star last Monday indicating that Pickering had been chosen as the site for the new international airport, I was disturbed. I knew interest had been displayed in the site. However, on calling the minister's office, I learned that no decision had been made.
Another r^Sson for establishing a committee to look into this matter is that such a committee would stop speculation. As I suggested, the longer this process goes on the greater the number of areas of the province will be considered. People will start buying little bits of land here and there in the hope of making tremendous profits in case any particular piece of land is chosen for the airport.
I have always been interested in seeing that railroads that serve my particular area are maintained. However, four years ago the Canadian Transport Commission autocratically decided to remove all passenger service in my region north and west of Guelph and west of Stratford. This has been a slow growth area, and rail service is important to it. By removing the service, the possibility of growth and increase in the area is removed. When people want to establish a factory in any area, they first ask, "What kind of transportation is there in the area?" I raised this matter in the committee last year. I was sorry that the Air Canada strike made it impossible for the Committee on Transport and Communications to go to western Ontario and look at the situation first hand, because I do not think the decision to remove that train service was a valid one.
The regulations under the National Transportation Act provide that before any passenger train service can be removed there must be evidence of good alternative service. At the meeting in Owen Sound it was thought that the assurance there would be alternative service had been given. However, the bus service is inadequate. The service that is provided for most of the area is inadequate and inefficient, and has not improved transportation facilities in that part of western Ontario. I am concerned especially about elderly people who cannot drive their cars and who must use existing services. There may be a good bus service on the eastern side of the area; I concede that. However, an equal service has not been developed on the western side of this particular area. I feel that the committee in question should be set up as soon as possible to look into this whole matter. If possible, arrangements should be made for it to go to the area to hear the tremendous number of briefs which many people have prepared. So far, these briefs have not been used.
The committee could not make its trip to western Ontario because of the air strike. So, Mr. Speaker, I hope that this committee will meet soon and will consider the motion that was passed in the previous session of parliament. I think that a similar motion will be accepted by the
Speech from the Throne
House in the present session, and the committee will be able to go to western Ontario and look at the transport problems of the area. I am referring to the problem relating to passenger transportation. I hope the committee can assure the people of the area that adequate transportation facilities will be set up.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, it has been a pleasure to represent my constituents in the House of Commons. I feel, as I have tried to indicate, that given the situation that has developed in Canada and the trends which are being shown not only in my riding but right across the nation, after the next election the member who will come down in my place, as well as those who are sitting with me on this side of House, will be sitting on the government side, and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) will be prime minister of Canada.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: But not "and Howe"!

speakerposition: Whip of the Social Credit Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the first place I must congratulate the mover and seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. The hon. members from Bruce and Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Wicher and Mr. Lajoie) performed their task well, in view of the difficulty of commending the government while remaining realistic.
In his speech of February 18 last, the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) who most evidently sought to defend his government under general attack, attempted to convince us that all is as well as can be in Canada. For instance, he resorted to statistics to show that Canada had created more jobs than seven countries of Europe together, namely France, Germany. Belgium, Italy, the Netherlands, Sweden and Great Britain.
Mr. Speaker, it is quite easy to create jobs when hundreds of thousands of workers are unemployed, but when countries enjoy a low unemployment rate and have a shortage of labour, how can industry, or even governments, create jobs?
Mr. Speaker, we did hear the government state that they had found a solution to unemployment through development of new projects such as Opportunities for Youth, the Local Initiatives Program, and Regional Economic Expansion, which can be called the second election fund of the Liberal party, but all these dishonest plans will have cost Canadian taxpayers millions of dollars in order to convince them that an attempt is being made to find solutions to their problems.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You rejected them.

speakerposition: Whip of the Social Credit Party
speechtext: I would ask the minister to repeat what he said as I did not understand.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I was asking the hon. member whether those projects were rejected in his constituency, whether he recommended that his constituents refuse to participate in the Opportunities for Youth, Local Initiatives and

February 25, 1972
Speech from the Throne
Regional Development programs for the reason he has just given, that these programs were dishonest.

speakerposition: Whip of the Social Credit Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, to reply to the minister, when you can't have what you want, you take what is available.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Even if it is dishonest?

speakerposition: Whip of the Social Credit Party
speechtext:
That is just what the Liberal party is doing now. That is not what people want. They want something else, not the loans now being granted. Canadians will have to pay interest on the debts resulting from all those projects. We will never live long enough in Canada to pay off ail those debts, or even the interest on them. That is the reason for my objections to those programs.
According to the National Institute Economic Review, published in March 1971, Canada is the greatest champion of unemployment, as compared with the above-mentioned countries. Western Germany, which was devastated by the World War II, has the lowest unemployment rate

0.7 per cent-whereas Canada's is 5.9 per cent, counting only registered claimants, and perhaps 7 to 8 per cent counting all unemployed persons.
What were the results of the promises made by the Liberal Party in 1968 for a just society?
We can therefore infer that unemployment exists not only among young people, although it is higher for them. Unemployment is increasing among workers of all ages and of both sexes.
A publication by Statistics Canada, dated September 1971 and titled ''Unemployment Data" shows interesting figures on unemployment, besides indicating that since the Liberal Party came into power in 1968, unemployment has kept rising steadily in all sectors of the population, I quote:
BOTH SEXES	1965	1970Age 14-19	65,000	117,000Age 20-24	44,000	107,000Age 25-44	93,000	157,000Age 45-64	70,000	106,000MEN	Age 14-19	43,000	74,000Age 20-24	33,000	80,000Age 25-44	78,000	125,000Age 45-64	61,000	87,000WOMEN	Age 14-19	22,000	42,000Age 20-24	11,000	27,000Age 25-44	15,000	32,000Age 45-64	8,000	19,000
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister tries very hard, the ministers distribute gifts right and left to create thousands of useless and non-productive jobs; still, unemployment keeps going up in Canada. Amongst the young of 14 to 24, as well as amongst the workers of 25 or more, the rate of unemployment has grown increasingly in Canada since 1968, when the Liberal government came to power.
Mr. Speaker, recently I received a card-which my colleagues doubtless received as well-sent by Le Cheminot canadien and asking that pressures be made upon the government to obtain full employment. Here is what the card said:
An act on full employment guaranteeing all Canadians who are able and willing to work a job suited to their competence and skills and paying a decent wage.
Mr. Speaker, as my leader said recently, instead of calling for guaranteed full employment for all Canadians, that card should have called for a guaranteed salary for each and every Canadian, which is what Social Credit advocates.
Mr. Speaker, the Liberals seem to find that funny; however, we shall certainly have to change our system. There is talk of providing full employment, but if there is no work now, it is because we have too many products in Canada. Even if Canada has 600,000 jobless, production is abundant. Stores are full of goods. In Ottawa or Hull, in my own region, Lac Saint-Jean, everywhere, stores are filled to capacity, and they say: We musLprovide jobs. How can this be achieved when there is*a surplus of products? There is the problem. That is why the Credi-tistes are calling for a guaranteed income for everybody. We must increase the purchasing power, so that people may purchase already existing products. Then, manufacturers will increase their production and everybody will be happy. This is what this government must consider.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The situation is quite the opposite. Inventories are lower than ever and this is why imports have increased.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member has the floor and should not be interrupted.

speakerposition: Whip of the Social Credit Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. minister will probably have a chance to explain himself later on.
I went to my constituency of Chibougamau where 450 miners have been on strike since December 18, 1971.1 met a sizeable group of strikers and they asked me if the provincial and federal governments could not help them. I have done my utmost to get something for those strikers, but to no avail. They are getting $20 a week plus $2 per child to live in Chibougamau. Thus a family of five is getting $30 a week. Of course neither the provincial nor the federal government is to blame for those people being on strike. However, if a dog is not allowed to starve neither should we allow our citizens to starve. Yesterday I received a petition asking me to do something. Those people are in a bad spot. My leader, the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette), stated in one of his speeches that Canada should ban all strikes and that they should be settled by a council comprising union representatives, government officials and company executives.
This morning, I was listening to one of my colleagues who quoted the following statement by Mr. George Meany:
Strikes today just don't make sense.
That is a man who controls 16 million workers in the AFL-CIO.
Mr. Speaker, it is something quite new for a labour leader to make such a statement. However, I find it very logical, because in the province of Quebec itself, that is in Montreal, a traffic problem exists. People's lives are in danger, just because a strike has not been settled.
(Mr. Pepin.]
February 25, 1972

Mr. Speaker, the Throne Speech dealt with our international relations. I wonder what purpose such relations have served, if not to give rise to a large number of interest-free loans, not to say gifts to some countries. Yet, our country should, through the Bank of Canada, grant some credit based on national values and the initiatives of Canadians. My colleagues and I have often said this but, apparently, the hon. members opposite do not want to hear!
On October 21, 1971, an opposition day allotted to my party, my colleague the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) moved a motion, that I myself seconded, for the payment of the old age security pension at age 60, as well as to the wife of a retired person, whatever her age.
I stated on that occasion that in my riding I had come across many cases where married older citizens received only $135 a month because their wives did not have the age required to get a pension. This situation continues to be a daily occurrence. As recently as yesterday I received a letter about a similar case. What can you tell those poor people except that their situation is due to a government without understanding or concern. It is not an act of charity for the government to give our older people a reasonnable pension.
Mr. Speaker, what I am saying might sound rather pessimistic but, realistic as I am, I can only see this situation as being very gloomy.
This is where the Trudeaumania that prevailed in the 1968 election has brought us but this swollen prestige will surely be deflated in the next election. I am very cheerful when I think that for the first time in 100 years we will no longer have puppets to head Canada's government.
Mr. Speaker, I spoke a while ago about our national debt. I have here a newspaper clipping giving rather interesting figures on the subject of our debt. This article goes back to 1970.	.

Mr. Speaker, I join with my colleagues to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the Address in reply. They are a credit to the House, to their ridings and to their party.
I intend today to give an account of the measures taken by the government, since 1965, to do away with regional disparity in Canada.
Speech from the Throne
When the expenditures of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion were under consideration on March 29, 1971, the minister (Mr. Jean Marchand) stated, and I quote:
When the department was established, I admitted that it would face considerable difficulties. A complete re-organization of what had been the basis of the Canadian economy for a century was required. I figured at the time that fifteen years would be required to effect such changes and to give them a solid foundation. We have, for a long time, been aware of the considerable unequality which exists between the people of the various regions of the country.
However to do away with that, and to establish sound conditions which would ensure the progress of the whole of the Canadian people is not a task that can be done quickly. To say that one or two years are enough would not serve the interest of the Canadian people. To attain our objectives, we must consider our long-term economic potential and envisage social changes in a long-range perspective. Considering, however, the extent of the task, it is of the utmost importance that we act as rapidly as possible and in the most realistic manner possible. As a matter of fact, it is only in this way that we can ensure the development of our country and, in truth, its survival.
Mr. Speaker, I have quoted this statement in order to inform the House of the objectives of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion.
I am not trying to overstate the economic progress made in the Gaspe riding, and I urge the government to pursue its efforts.
I want to assure Canadians from prosperous areas that funds allocated by the government to regional development of the Gaspe peninsula and eastern Quebec have had good results, and I can show that there has been a real start upward in the area which I represent in this House.
In spite of a certain slowdown in the North American economy, the economic development of the Gaspe peninsula has progressed considerably, If the economic situation had continued in Canada after centennial year things would have been very different in eastern Quebec, particularly in connection with implementation of regional development programs. Even so, the unemployment rate is no higher in 1972 than it was back in 1963 when the Progressive Conservatives were in power.
The Gaspe area is recovering from a long illness, and the remedies provided by legislation concerning economic incentives, and especially by the new Department of Regional Economic Expansion, have contributed a great deal to its development.
The reforms proposed in order to reduce administrative costs at all levels of government have been accepted, and the population now recognizes the value of grouping services in centres and subcentres defined on the basis of economic or geographical considerations.
In the Gaspe Peninsula, and more specifically in my riding, six hamlets were closed down and most of the 225 families involved as well as the 220 households which were relocated as a result of the expropriations for Foril-lon park were moved to the designated service centres. The contribution of the government of Canada toward the purchase of the lands, the relocation grants and the housing subsidies to the families that lived in the hamlets and Forillon park now amount to over $10 million.
In conjunction with the development of the service centres, two hospitals were built thanks to a federal contribu-

Speech from the Throne
tion of $1.5 million, and three composite high schools, thanks to another federal contribution of $2,138,000. Grants totalling $1.5 million were made for the construction of low rental housing units in the designated centres to enable the relocalization of those same people. Millions of dollars in grants also went toward the construction of water and sewage systems in the designated centres.
The Department of Public Works and FRED also granted over $8 million for the construction of fishing wharves and harbours.
With regard to the construction of the Gaspe airport, which cost $878,000, the government has just granted the town of Gaspe a subsidy of $210,000 for the construction of an air terminal, this through the winter works program of the Department of Transport. With regard to the highway system, since 1964 Ottawa has granted a subsidy of $13 million for repairs to Highway 6 located partly in the riding of Gaspe and partly in that of Matane. In addition, a $2 million subsidy was earmarked for building access roads to natural resources, which resulted in 1969 in the setting up of a new mining industry near Sainte-Anne-des Monts, by the McIntyre mining interests which invested $14 million in that new plant. That new plant now provides employment for 200 workers with a total annual salary of $1.6 million.
The production of Mines Madeleine Limitee during the first year of operation was about 20 million pounds of copper and 200,000 ounces of silver. Refined metal at this new plant accounts for a yearly gross value of $11.7 million. The Mines Madeleine Limitee contributed-greatly to the economic and social recovery of the northern part of the Gaspe peninsula and I advise the directors of the McIntyre Mines Group to keep on with their prospection, in order to find other resources in the Gaspe subsoil.
With the help of subsidies from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and the collaboration from the province of Quebec, Noranda Mines Limited undertook last year improvements of $110 million in its Gaspe Copper Mines Plants. It is estimated that the number of new permanent jobs that will be created in Murdochville, once the program is implemented, will increase by 280. The work should be completed by the end of 1973. The Gaspe inhabitants are grateful to the Noranda Mines Limited group who chose Murdochville as the site of those new plants and I hope that the eventual establishment of a copper refining plant in the Gaspe area is still being considered.
The Gaspesia Pulp and Paper Ltd Company, in Chandler, put in in 1968 a second newsprint machine, following a contribution from the federal government and economic incentives of about $2.7 million.
Mr. Speaker, the pulp and paper industry has already contributed very much to the economic activity in the povince of Quebec, but in the last few years-and everyone agrees-the pulp and paper producers have had a hard time because of stronger competition. Our costs are no longer competitive and some of our plants are no longer profitable.
In Gaspe, the Gaspesia Pulp and Paper Company Limited, from 1960 to 1971, invested $3.27 million for lumber operations, in order to improve its system, and $40.6 million in its Chandler plant, for the purchase of two news-

print machines, as well as for other capital outlays and also major repairs to its equipment, all this in order to produce newsprint instead of commercial pulp. The joint owners of the company, the New York Times, purchase 60 per cent of its annual production.
If some economists or politicians criticize the pulp and paper companies, holding them partly responsible for the present situation as a result of their lack of planning, such charges indeed do not apply to the directors of the Gaspesia Pulp and Paper Company Limited, in Chandler, since that company has streamlined its operation and its production in order to make its plant one of the best organized in the province. And I believe that those who achieved it should be commended.
Still under the same topic, that of regional development, I must say that two sawmills are presently under construction, one in Grande-Vallee and the other in Marsoui. The establishment of those two sawmills in my constituency would have been impossible without grants of about $956,000 from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion.
As concerns fisheries, the federal government contributed $2 million in 1967 for the organization of the fishing complex in Riviere-au-Renard, one of the most modern in eastern Canada.
For a fish-hatchery which is being built at Anse-Pleureuse, a $578,750 grant covering 75 per cent of its capital cost was allowed by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion under FRED.
Mr. Speaker, in the Speech from the Throne reference is made to a policy designed to promote the tourist industry in this country, as well as the expansion of our network of national parks, and the assurance that vast areas of Canada will be preserved in their natural state for the enjoyment of this and future generations.
In Gaspe, we started off several years ago. We already have our Forillon National Park, tourist areas at Perce, Carleton and Mont-Saint-Pierre, thanks to the co-operation of the federal government. And I am deeply grateful to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) and to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) as well for those developments.
Under FRED, $2 million have been granted to the province to share in the development of the tourist areas in my constituency, that is Mont-Saint-Pierre and Perce, in addition to a sum of $350,000 affected by the federal Department of Environment for the construction of a wildlife interpretation centre in Perce, the second one in Canada, and work will be undertaken on March 1.
The Gaspe peninsula will undergo considerable economic development, thanks to the creation of the Forillon national park. It is expected indeed that the number of tourists in the Gaspe peninsula, which has levelled at 225,000 persons these past few years, will have tripled in 1976 to reach 700,000 visitors. As a result, there will be an annual cash input of some $42 million. The work in that park began in 1969 and in five or seven years, over $10 million will have been invested.
Mr. Speaker, that co-operation of the federal government since 1965 must not come to an end. Indeed, it must continue, and my statement confirms what His Excellency
February 25, 1972

the Governor General said on February 17, 1972 in the Speech from the Throne and I quote:
-the government has worked to strengthen and promote the economies of the less developed regions of Canada.
I must congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his cabinet.
Without the financial assistance of the federal government to regional development and the excellent co-operation of Quebec, all these achievements and several others still would have been nothing but a dream.
He who cannot recognize that there is in Gaspe a new start, thanks to the efforts of both governments, is blind. We shall always have some frustrated people, some malcontents, even if we pay them a trip to the moon, because they cannot adjust to change.
To end this retrospective, I wish to pay a tribute to the people of Gaspe and, in particular, to the municipal administrations, Chambers of Commerce and citizens' committees for their co-operation in these social and economic changes which have occurred in my riding. They all worked together in harmony and always suggested concrete and realistic solutions. Everything went on in a peaceful instead of a fighting mood.
Gaspesians are grateful to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion and to all federal and provincial public servants for the interest they show for this tremendous development in our area.
Mr. Speaker, on another occasion I will have the opportunity to draw to your attention the concern showed by the Minister of Environment (Mr. Davis) for the development of our fisheries and the conservation of our marine resources.
I would now like to inform the House and Canadians of the recent Canada-Quebec agreement for the economic and social development of Eastern Quebec.
In October 1971, after the Canada-Quebec agreement had been signed, two British Columbia ministers, that is the Hon. Dan Campbell, Minister of Municipal Affairs, and the Hon. Ray. Williston, Minister of Lands and Forests, sent a letter to the mayors of Vancouver Island, suggesting that Ottawa was spending an additional $400 million in the Gaspe, and criticizing the federal regional development policy in doing so.
In that circular letter to the mayors of that area, Mr. Campbell says, and I quote:
As you will remember, in part the case was made on the basis of activities carried on by this particular federal department in other areas of Canada and the case was made that British Columbia certainly deserved equal treatment. I now have on hand another example which makes the present federal policy equally discriminatory. Indeed, when one considers that this most recent program is over and above any equalization payments or special deals the fact that discrimination exists becomes overwhelmingly clear.
In addition, in terms of the area involved with this particular program, a strong case can be made that this recent agreement is another example of the mismanagement of capital on a colossal scale. If one examines a $400,000,000 expenditure over 5 years assigned to an area which has a population of 220,000 one cannot help but express amazement that such an expenditure could be contemplated.
Speech from the Throne

In his letter of October 5, 1971 to Mr. H. A. Moffat, mayor of Prince George, Mr. Williston said, and I quote:

Within the last couple of weeks a new program of assistance has been announced for the Gaspe region of Quebec. This marks a second attempt when a first program became bogged down after the spending of something more than one hundred million dollars on the paperwork without a development involving any physical accomplishment. The new five-year program commits the expenditure of four hundred eleven million dollars. The population to receive such assistance numbers about 240,000 people.
It is not my purpose to show that assistance should not be extended to the people in this section of Quebec. However, I do think that if there is this type of money available for help that the presentations made by both the province and the municipalities from British Columbia are worthy of some type of positive response. I am sure that if we do not protest the lack of fair treatment for our own people that we can be accused of poor representation on their behalf.

Mr. Speaker, referring to this Canada-Quebec agreement, I should note that it is not exclusively for the benefit of the Gaspe Peninsula, but also for the benefit of eastern Quebec and Magdalene Islands. The financial contribution of the government of Canada to this agreement is of assistance to our region but not to the prejudice of other provinces.
As I pointed out, this agreement does not affect only the Gaspe Peninsula but covers a territory of 17,000 square miles with a population of 335,000 and comprises ten provincial constituencies and six federal ridings.
It should be noted that the combined area of Vancouver Island and Prince Edward Island-12,000 and 2,000 square miles, respectively-is smaller than that of the eastern Quebec territory covered by the agreement. Let us now see what the overall objective of this agreement is.
The main industries in the region are forestry, mines, fisheries, tourism and agriculture. The major objective in these fields of activity is to raise the income of the people and to increase productivity in primary industries, which are the regional economic mainstay, through a training programme for adult manpower.
Let us examine these programs at length: That agreement provides for the integration and co-ordination of routine activities within various federal and provincial departments. This explains the inclusion, in whole or in part, of the regular budgets of several departments in this $411 million vote to which the province of Quebec is contributing $113,588,000.
The agreement provides for planned assistance to industrial development, urban infrastructures and transportation, but all in terms of each department's regular programs, in addition to a supplement of $153 million from the department of Regional Economic Expansion for a period of five years, thus representing a yearly contribution of $36 millions in new votes or $108 a year per capita.
The first agreement was signed in May 1968 for a five-year period and for an amount of $258,790,000, including federal and provincial contributions.

How much have British Columbia and the western provinces received from the federal government for parks and historical sites in 105 years?
According to a report supplied to me by the Department of Indian Affairs, British Columbia has three national parks. In capital investment to operate those parks, the National Parks Branch has spent $14,620,763 from 1961 to 1971, and the maintenance expenses amounted to $11,659,000 from 1966 to 1971.
In the province of Quebec, we are proceeding with the first national park at Forillon, and in British Columbia, they are proceeding at this time with the fourth national park, which will be named the Pacific Rim Park. If there is discrimination as far as parks are concerned, it is surely not in British Columbia.
As to fisheries, the agreement provides, as I said earlier, for $4,200,000 to be earmarked for the building of fishing boats, out of the program which calls for a grant of 35 per cent from this government.
Considering that British Columbia has the biggest fishing fleet in Canada, the fishermen of that province will

certainly receive greater subsidies than those of Quebec under that program.
This shows, Mr. Speaker, that all the regular programs of federal departments are included in that "Canada-Que-bec Agreement".
It is obvious from the table which I have quoted that the people of the Lower St. Lawrence, the Gaspe peninsula and Iles-de-la-Madeleine-and I see the hon. member from Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bechard) is here- are no more favoured than those of other depressed areas in the country, such as Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
The statements made by the ministers of the British Columbia government on the "Canada-Quebec Agreement", as well as the recent attacks of the Attorney General of that province, the Hon. Leslie Patterson, who tries to question the constitutionality of equalization payments made to certain provinces, demonstrate the mentality of some politicians who seem to favor the creation of two classes of Canadians, by approving of poverty for some and accumulating wealth for others.
It is difficult to understand how ministers in a province like British Columbia can possibly send such mistaken letters to city councils. Had they only gone to the trouble of first asking for information from their devoted representatives, ministers or even backbenchers of the government party who come from that province, they would have obtained it and would thus have avoided another quarrel between eastern and western Canada. If this is the policy of the British Columbia Social Credit party, it is lamentable.
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne states that the government is concerned about the fact that several communities are presently deprived of national broadcasting services and that about a million Canadians in some 260 localities have no television broadcasting service in their own language. The Government proposes, therefore, that the C.B.C. be authorized to extend its services in a comprehensive fashion and to utilize the capabilities of Canada's pioneer satellite communications system to assure within a five year period that at least 98 percent of Canadians are served.
I wish to congratulate the government for this initiative as a large percentage of the people in my riding do not have access to television programs.
Television has been in Canada for the past 20 years and it is a sad thing to realize that in certain areas, some families in order to get service in the first place have to buy from a group a $100 share in the cable television and afterwards they have to pay a monthly charge of up to $8.
On several occasions, I have met the Canadian RadioTelevision Commission directors. Last year the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) came to Gaspe to assess the situation. I am happy to see that the CRTC maintains its priority requirements for distant places such as the Gaspe peninsula.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the speech made yesterday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), his first speech in the House since he was dragooned into accepting that post. As I listened, I could not help but feel sorry for the minister. Here he is, young, handsome and wealthy, a completely bilingual Member of Parliament who wants-and I cannot blame him-to be prime minister of Canada when that post becomes open. When he yvas minister of justice he was able to change the bail procedures and propose legislation to outlaw wiretapping, issues which are certainly important to people like myself who believe in civil liberties but which are not the tremendous concern of the bulk of the Canadian people. These issues permitted him to project the image of being progressive and small "1" liberal.
Now, unfortunately for the Minister of Finance, he has been asked to take on a position which requires him to give the lead, to give the direction in which our economy will move in the next couple of years. The voice we heard yesterday was the voice of the Minister of Finance, just as the voice we heard in the past three or four years was the voice of the former minister of finance, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Mr. Benson); but the words and thoughts expressed both in the speech yesterday and in the speeches of the former minister were the words and thoughts of the deputy minister of finance.
Over the years in which the former minister of finance held that position he made innumerable predictions, to which I will come back in a few moments, about how we were on the threshold of improving conditions so that unemployment would be reduced and the needs of the people met. Those predictions proved to be as false as the explanations of the minister were lengthy.
As I listened to the Minister of Finance speaking yesterday I found in his speech not a single new idea. There were some new words, and some new concerns were expressed which were good to hear, but there was not a single indication that the policies of the government have changed. So while the speech yesterday did not sound bad, and the speech in March will not sound bad, when we get to September, October, November and December of 1972 and the unemployment rates will not be much better than they are at present, the credibility of the Minister of Finance will disappear in the same way as the credibility of the former minister disappeared. When that happens, I am afraid that the opportunity of this Minister of Finance to become prime minister of Canada at some time in the future will disappear just as the snow in Ottawa and Winnipeg will disappear in the next couple of weeks or months.
Speech from, the Throne
Let me quote a couple of paragraphs from the speech made yesterday by the Minister of Finance. He said:
Despite substantial progress in developing policies and mechanisms for guiding the economy, it still remains difficult to determine with precision the state of the economy and its direction at any given time. It follows that there are always difficulties in determining what levers should be pulled, with what force, and at what exact time, in order to bring about a correction in the course of the economy.
I submit that the economic advisers of this government, the deputy minister of finance, the governor of the Bank of Canada, the chairman of the unlamented Prices and Incomes Commission, and the secretary of the Treasury Board knew what was going to happen in the last couple of years. They knew what was going to happen in the last couple of years, Mr. Speaker, because they had the same information as other economists across the country. If one looks at the record it can be seen that economists like Professor Weldon of McGill University, Professor Blauer of Brock University and Dian Cohen who writes a column in the Toronto Star, as well as some of the best economists in the province of Quebec, were predicting precisely what would happen and saying that the policies adopted by the government would lead to the situation which we are in at the present.
Mr. Speaker, the government advisers, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the then minister of finance knew what would happen. The events that took place were not an accident, not the result of ignorance but the result of deliberate choices made by the government and its advisers. The priorities set by the government showed that they believed that the problem which had to be faced in this country was inflation and they set out to deal with it, even if only temporarily. As a result, the economists I have mentioned predicted greater unemployment. Yesterday in the House the minister said:
Throughout most of the 1960s the Canadian economy experienced the greatest period of sustained expansion in its history.
He left the impression that most Canadians benefited from that expansion. I have here a document entitled "Our Tomorrows", prepared by the Indian tribes of Manitoba and published in October, 1971. I should like to give a couple of illustrations of the situation in Manitoba regarding Indians who do not live in my constituency. I am not putting their plight on the record because I am not making a plea for people whom I personally represent, but I should like to quote from this document a couple of illustrations of their situation. At page 47 it reads:
The infant mortality rate for Indian people is twice as high as that for the general population (including Indians) of Manitoba. Mortality among young adults is four times that of this general population. The Manitoba Indian population's morbidity rate from tuberculosis is appalling in itself, and ten times that of the general population (again including Indians).
Later, talking about the income of Indians, it reads at page 51:
To indicate the extent of this poverty of the 32 per cent of employables living on reserves, male and female, ages 15-64 who have an earned income, only 4 per cent earned in excess of $4,000 in 1969. The balance of the population must depend completely or in part on social allowances or other state support.
