Speech from the Throne
Mr. Speaker, those facts ought to make every Member of Parliament and every Canadian citizen ashamed of the system which we have allowed to grow and exist in Canada. Later in his speech the Minister of Finance said:
Since the fall of 1970, the growth of our economy has been accelerating in response to the progressively stronger stimulus injected by the federal government-
Well, Mr. Speaker, those of us who oppose the government's economic policy of trying to deal with inflation as its number one priority were calling on the government to implement expansionary policies for at least 18 months before it adopted them. Later in his speech the Minister of Finance said something which sounded a little different from the views of his predecessor. He said:
Our most urgent and pressing task is to bring about a substantial reduction in the level of unemployment. Our goal, our objective, must be the provision of a job to every Canadian who is seeking work.
That sounds great, Mr. Speaker, but the record of this government should not give the people of Canada the right to feel that this government intends to take steps to achieve that end. I have said that the minister, I am sure on the advice of the deputy minister who certainly is not living in a state of poverty, goes back to the old argument put forward by the Prime Minister and the former minister of finance, and so we are back where we have been for the last three years. The minister then said:
This leads me to what in my judgment is the fundamental problem of economic management. This is the problem of maintaining maximum growth of employment and production in the economy, while at the same time preventing the development of inflationary pressures which eventually could undermine the very foundations of the economy if allowed to go unchecked.
It was that kind of thinking which led the government to adopt its policies of restraint which have resulted in unemployment in Canada in the four Trudeau years being twice as high as it was in the four Pearson years.
As high as under the Conservatives.

My colleague from Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Mather) says "As high as under the Conservatives," but he is wrong, Mr. Speaker. It is much higher than it was under the Conservatives. I want to put on record again the fact that we have heard these promises and pledges from the representatives of government for the last couple of hears, to the effect that things would get better. I would say, Mr. Speaker, that I have heard them ad nauseam. Let me put on the record a couple of examples of the promises and pledges. On November 12, 1970, the then minister of finance said:
Recently I suggested publicly that on a seasonal basis .. unemployment had about reached its peak and expressed confidence that we could look forward to continued improvement.
When he made that statement we had an unemployment rate, seasonally adjusted, of 6.5 per cent. Some 14 months later, in January, 1972, it was 6.2 per cent. But he was not alone, Mr. Speaker. On March 18, 1971, the Prime Minister said:
The government has taken a series of steps intended to alter the course of the economic policy ... Some time must elapse before these steps can be fully efficient.

Then he said:
I think that all the economic indicators show that the economy is moving.
When the Prime Minister said that in March, 1971, the rate of unemployment was 6.2 per cent, precisely what it was eight months later in January, 1972. Then in April, 1971, the then parliamentary secretary to the then minister of finance said:
The government is not prepared to accept an unemployment rate of 5 per cent to 6 per cent seasonally adjusted or otherwise, for the future.
That was in April of last year, Mr. Speaker, and here we are, not with an unemployment rate of 5.5 or 6 per cent but with one of 6.2 per cent. I say that there was not a single indication in the speech the Minister of Finance made yesterday to indicate that the government has realized that the policies it has followed for so long are wrong and doomed to failure. The government's policies will continue to fail so long as the government refuses to face the reasons leading to unemployment and to adopt policies which must be adopted if we are to get rid of unemployment and the suffering which results from unemployment.
A couple of weeks ago we saw the figures which are issued each month by Statistics Canada showing unemployment for the previous month. Like most newspapers across Canada, the Globe and Mail carried a sypnosis of the statistics issued by Statistics Canada; it appeared in an article on February 9. Let me put on record what the situation was at that time. I am referring to the figures for January, 1972. There were 665,000 Canadians out of work in January this year, 135,000 more than in December of 1971 but 3,000 less than in January, 1971.
The number of unemployed this past January represented 7.7 per cent of the labour force. In January, 1971, the actual rate of unemployment was 8 per cent. So there was a reduction of .3 per cent, in other words one-third of 1 per cent. The rate of unemployment, after adjustment for the usual seasonal causes, declined to 6.2 per cent in January, 1972, from 6.3 per cent in December, 1971, and 6.4 per cent in January, 1971. In other words, between January, 1972, and January one year earlier, unemployment declined by one-fifth of 1 per cent. The number of unemployed increased substantially in the Atlantic provinces which traditionally suffer the heaviest rate of unemployment. Unemployment remained almost constant in Quebec, a province which has too much unemployment, and remained quite heavy in the prairie provinces.
How did we get in this mess? The government and the Prime Minister of course deny that they are responsible for unemployment, that it was their deliberate policies which created the present substantial rate of unemployment. It sometimes seems to me that the government has adopted a basic principle which was adopted successfully in some totalitarian countries before and during World War II, the principle that if you tell a lie often enough it will become a truth and you can rewrite history.
Just before Christmas-in December, 1970-when interviewed and asked how serious he was about the government's policy of restraint designed to curb the rising cost of living, the Prime Minister said something like, "Just
February 25, 1972

watch me. I will not be deterred from this policy even if the result of this policy leads to an unemployment rate of 6 per cent." Well, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister was successful and even more than successful. He succeeded, as he said he would and as his ministers have repeatedly reminded us, in bringing the increase in the cost of living in 1970 to a virtual standstill. In 1970 the cost of living increased by less than 2 per cent. Of course, what the Prime Minister did not tell us then and what he now tries to deny is that the policies the government adopted would inevitably lead to a sharp increase in the number of unemployed.
When the government announced these policies, not only opposition members but economists across the country predicted precisely what would happen and it has happened. Those economists who predicted that the measures taken by the government to control increases in living costs would mean much higher unemployment also said that no country, and certainly not a country like Canada which is so dependent on its sales to and purchases from the United States, could insulate itself from the effects of inflation in the United States. So although the government was successful in holding the line, in holding down living cost increases in 1970-a policy which, as I say, inevitably brought about sharply increased unemployment-the success of the government was temporary because what happened afterwards was precisely what economists had predicted.
In 1971 the cost of living rose by 5 per cent, the largest annual increase in our cost of living in a decade. That was the direct result of the Trudeau government's economic policies. In 1971 they brought about the sharpest increase in the cost of living and the highest unemployment to be seen in this country for more than a decade. And what of the future, Mr. Speaker? Yesterday the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) made the usual promises about prosperity being just around the corner. I almost expected to hear the famous prediction which Herbert Hoover made when he was President of the United States during the depression. He said it would not be long before everyone had two chickens in the pot.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: He did not say disaster was just around the corner.
I beg your pardon, Mr. Speaker; I did not hear that gem.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: He did not say disaster was just around the corner.

I do not say disaster is around the corner. I am not suggesting for a moment that we are going back to the thirties. Surely nobody, not even the most moss-backed Tory, can fail to recognize that we have built into the economy many stabilizing factors which will prevent our going back to the condition of the 1930s when one-third of the Canadian people were unemployed and perhaps even more were on welfare, or relief as it was then called.
Only a Prime Minister with a computer where his heart should be could think we are not doing badly when 6.2 per cent of the work force of this country is unemployed. Only
Speech from the Throne
a Prime Minister who has never had to work for a living could ignore the results that unemployment brings to the paper worker or the textile worker of Quebec, who has not been unemployed in the way that Indians on the reserves of Manitoba, who have never had a chance to work, have been unemployed. The workers I am talking about have had jobs for the last 10, 15 or 20 years. They expected their jobs to continue and based their expectations on continued employment. I am talking about workers in Sudbury who are being laid off.
Just a couple of months ago the Prime Minister was telling the people of Canada that there were all kinds of jobs. He said, if you do not have a job in Montreal or Toronto, go to Thompson, Manitoba, or Sudbury, Ontario, where there are all kinds of jobs in the mines and smelters for people who want to work. A couple of weeks after the Prime Minister made that ridiculous statement, International Nickel announced it was laying off between 2,000 and 2,500 workers. I want the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) to tell the people who have been laid off in Thompson, in Sudbury and in his constituency how they are going to meet the payments on the house, automobile and television set which they bought because they thought they had secure jobs. Only a cabinet of millionaires and technocrats can have this kind of contempt for people who are poor and unemployed.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Millionaire? Me?

I exempt the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce from the list of millionaires. However, he knows who they are. There are many such people in this government.
It is all very well for ministers such as the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to make glowing predictions about what is going to happen and to say that things will become better and better. However, the Economic Council of Canada, as reported in the February 23 edition of the Globe and Mail, predicted a slowdown in capital spending. I suggest to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce that if one wants to know what is likely to happen in the year ahead, he should not look at the propaganda speeches made by ministers or the gloom and doom speeches made by members of the opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Nor by the Economic Council.

The minister interjected, "Nor by the Economic Council". I say to the minister that the record speaks for itself. This country and this government would be a hell of a lot better off if the government had listened more to the Economic Council of Canada and less to the deputy minister of finance.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister may ask a question if the hon. member who has the floor agrees to accept it.

Yes, Mr. Speaker.

Speech from the Throne

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: If the hon. member wants to see me after he completes his remarks, I will show him all kinds of qualifications made by the Economic Council. They say the forecasting is not as good as the time framework expands. Their prognostication does not take into account housing, changes in the international economic conjuncture. The hon. member made the flat statement that the Economic Council of Canada said business investment will not be as good in 1976 as at the present time. The Economic Council of Canada qualified that and the hon. member has left out the qualifications. That is not fair.

Of course, the Economic Council-which is a body of responsible, independent and, I presume, objective economists-has added caveats to its projection. I suggest that if the deputy minister of finance would stop being a politician and stop writing all kinds of nonsense which this government wants-

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You are conveniently changing the subject.

-and began to be the economist he once was, the government would receive some of the advice it needs rather than the advice it wants. The government's projections as to future employment have been consistently wrong. I challenge the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to sit down with me-

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We are always wrong on the low side.

I challenge the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to sit down with me, at his convenience, to look at the projections which the government has made which are based on information they received from the deputy minister of finance and his assistants.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, from business.

I would like him to compare the predictions with those made by members of this party, predictions which we did not pull out of the air. We obtained these predictions from economists, the names of whom I would be more than willing to give to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I regret that I must interrupt the hon. member to advise him that his time has expired.
Continue.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps before I recognize the minister on a question I could determine whether there is consent to extend the time of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). Is it agreed?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I take it the hon. member for Winnipeg North will accept a question from the minister.
Yes, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Is the hon. member aware that my department carries out a forecasting of investment intentions every year which is based on information provided by

industry? Is he aware that they have been wrong nine times in the past 12 years, on the pessimistic side?
I presume when the minister says "they have been wrong", he means that his department has been wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: This is done on the basis of information provided to my department. Forecasting is a difficult art and when forecasting, businessmen, unfortunately, tend to be more "PC" than "Lib."

I am prepared to accept the minister's statement that his departmental officials have been wrong on the conservative side nine times out of 12. I ask the minister what this proves.
One statement made by the Minister of Finance gives me a small hope that maybe this Minister of Finance is adopting a new look at things. I want to point this out to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Yesterday the Minister of Finance said:
We can have a strong expansionary economy, a rising GNP, strong retail sales, strong consumer spending, together with intolerable rates of unemployment. It has become quite clear that optimistic statistics are no answer to human problems.
That is the kind of statement we on this side of the House have been making to the government for the past four years and which they have ignored. I want to put on record what the Economic Council said about capital spending, as reported in the Globe and Mail:
The survey-released yesterday-shows the real volume of capital spending on new buildings, machinery and equipment by 155 major business firms last year was 8.4 per cent below their year-earlier plans.
And-depending on which of two yardsticks, provided by the council, are used-it shows the firms are planning for 1972 at best a 3.6 per cent increase in real (constant dollar) volume of spending and at worst almost no change whatever from their depressed 1971 level of outlays.
"These capital investment intentions for 1972, followed by quite sharp declines, especially among business firms, in 1973 and for the balance of the survey period, represent a substantially weaker investment outlook than obtained in any previous capital investment survey conducted by the Economic Council of Canada"-
I hope, because I am concerned about the well being of the ordinary citizens of Canada, that the Economic Council is wrong. I hope there will be a great deal more capital spending.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: They qualified everything you are saying.
Of course they qualified their statements. I hope they are wrong.
They are not prophets; they are forecasters.

I say that the indications for the future are not good. Because the government has not really changed its approach, the prospects for meeting the problems of poverty and unemployment in the next couple of years remain very dark.
What is the basic question? It is on this note that I am going to close. I said earlier that the government chose its priorities. The government decided that the number one problem facing Canada with which it had to deal was that
February 25, 1972

of inflation. It was the fear it had of inflation which led the government to adopt its policies of restraint which created the high level of unemployment that we have. Inflation in Canada cannot be eliminated until inflation is licked in the United States. The economy gives us what we want. If we want to deal with inflation, we are going to have unemployment. You cannot stop rising costs and not have increased unemployment.
What determines the well being of this country, Mr. Speaker? I suggest there are two basic factors: firstly, the amount of expansion that we have in Canada-about this the government has a great deal of say through the policies it adopts-secondly, the amount of inflation there is in the United States.
While it is obvious we cannot do much about inflation in the United States, we can do a great deal about expanding the Canadian economy. Unfortunately, there was nothing in the speech yesterday of the Minister of Finance, and not a single word in his answers to several questions at the conclusion of his speech, to indicate that in fact-not just in words, but in action-the minister has decided we must change the direction in which the government is leading the country.
I say that until the Minister of Finance changes his approach and adopts the attitude that the first requirement of the government, any government in this country, is to provide a job for every single person who wants to work, and adopts specific economic policies to bring about that objective, we shall continue to have unemployment at a level unmatched in any country in the western world except the United States. We shall continue to have poverty. We shall continue to move, not toward that just society about which the Prime Minister spoke so eloquently in 1968 but away from the just society that should be the objective of every Member of Parliament and every Canadian.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul St. Pierre (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I, like others who have taken part in this debate, begin by congratulating the mover and the seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher) and the hon. member for Trois Rivieres (Mr. Lajoie). I was interested to note both these members, and several others who have spoken in this debate, expressed very favourable opinions of their home constituencies. I think this is welcome news because we all know that it is not everybody who can live in British Columbia, let alone that favoured portion, the riding of Coast-Chilcotin. While we welcome our fellows as visitors at all times, we know that our province is really not big enough to accommodate everybody.
In more serious vein, I think one of the better aspects of the life of a Member of Parliament is that most of us do from time to time get to see different areas in Canada and we realize, or we are reminded once again, that every one has its charm, its own traditions and its own pride. We see this exhibited in our travels and we see it exhibited in other ways in this House. And surely this is a good thing, because I believe that we as Members of Parliament are particularly aware that it is these little differences-like the little bit of difference that remains between the sexes-that makes life interesting.
Speech from the Throne
The fundamental things that Canadians hold in common with one another are stronger than any regional differences, even those differences that occasionally lead to family spats. I think the sense of identity as citizens of Canada becomes more apparent to Canadians when outside the borders of this country; the perspective is better from abroad. But I think there are very few, probably none, in this House who do not believe that the cement of the Canadian confederation's foundation is actually very strong.
These considerations lead me indirectly to the subject of my few remarks today. I am going to deal with one topic only. I do not intend to deal with the Throne Speech as a whole but to speak about one particular aspect of Canadian affairs with which I regret to say the Throne Speech did not deal. It is, I suggest, a thing that is badly needed. I refer to the reform of our immigration laws.
Canada must be one of the most hospitable nations of any, in terms of its immigration laws. There is nothing wrong with that sentiment, but I suggest that some people are abusing our hospitality. I refer in particular to some of those who enter this country as visitors, who then apply for citizenship while resident in Canada, who then appeal a negative decision and in many cases continue to live and work in this country with practically full rights while the overburdened Immigration Appeal Board attempts to deal with their case.
There are appeals that are legitimate, of course, and there are appeals that are not. But there can be no doubt that some of our visitors are treating us as patsies. Somewhere along the line our immigration law has perhaps lost sight of a fundamental principle, a very simple principle, namely, that no citizen of a foreign country can demand Canadian citizenship as an inherent right. Canadian citizenship is a privilege. Some of us are born with it; some of us acquired it. All of us who have it are equal. But however acquired, whether by birth or by naturalization, it is something valuable. It is something which, unless Canadians themselves treat it as something valuable, will diminish us in the eyes of others.
Before proceeding, Mr. Speaker, I should say that I regret that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mackasey) cannot be present today. As hon. members know, he is in hospital and I know that we all wish him a speedy return. My remarks, of course, are not directed toward him or his immediate predecessor: in my opinion it was some years ago that our immigration policy was altered in a way that proved to be at least a serious error of judgment if not a mistake in principle.
Some of the immigration law changes of some years ago were undoubtedly enlightened. In fact, most of them were. Certainly, I should not like it to be thought that I am suggesting we ever return to immigration laws that bar immigrants on the basis of skin colour or any other considerations of race. In this modern age, considerations of racial prejudice have no place in the laws of an enlightened state.
Nor do I think we should object to immigration laws permit the reuniting of close relatives. The points system, from my observation, is relatively fair. There might be debate as to whether too much weight is given to one or

February 25, 1972
Speech from the Throne
another aspect of an application in determining the number of points in accordance with the scale, but this is a matter of detail, not of principle. Humanitarian considerations must be a part of our immigration policy. Canadians would not want an immigration policy which was devoid of this principle. Again, I am in favour of the aspect of policy which requires that the number of immigrants who are job seekers should be scaled to the job situation in Canada at the time, category by category.
There are a few interesting figures which tell to some extent the story of immigration over recent years. Between 1967 and 1970, immigration into Canada dropped by 34 per cent, from 223,000 to 148,000. It is interesting, also, to take note of the general pattern of immigration in Canada as compared with that of similar developed countries. As a percentage per thousand of population, Canada admitted immigrants during the period of which I am speaking at a rate of 10.7. That was in 1967. The figure in 1969 was 6.9. The rate is higher than it is in the United States. In that country they had a fairly constant rate of 2 throughout the sixties. It was a little higher than the United Kingdom, where immigration rose from 4.1 in 1958 to 4.4 in 1968. However, it reverses the trend in Australia where in 1966 the rate amounted to 7.8 in 1966 and was up to 10.3 in 1969.
But why, I ask, Mr. Speaker, is Canada just about the only nation which allows visitors to apply for landed immigrant status without first returning to their country of origin and then coming back through the front door together with other immigrants? This practice of permitting appeals within Canada by people who have not gone through the standard procedure of applying outside our borders is unfair to other applicants abroad who accept the basic principles governing entry. Such appeals have swamped our Immigration Appeal Board. Their number has made the situation more difficult for legitimate applicants and it has begun to cause concern among citizens at home, some of whom are beginning to wonder whether Canadians are sufficiently masters in their own house.
I should like to quote a few further figures at this point. I regret they are not as up to date as one would wish; however, they cover the period to the end of July of last year and I have no reason to believe the situation has greatly altered since then. At that time the Immigration Appeal Board had a backlog of 6,771 cases. The board can hear approximately 90 or 100 cases a month. During the period in question they were receiving appeals at the rate of between 400 and 425 cases a month. The backlog, then, in July, 1971, amounted to seven year's worth of cases, each of which costs the taxpayer approximately $1,000.
About two-thirds of these appeals concern persons who entered as visitors and who then applied unsuccessfully for landed immigrant status. In the first three months of 1971, more than one-third of those who applied for landed immigrant status did so after having entered Canada as visitors. The figures are 11,514 out of 27,899. About a third of this 11,514-4,432-were Americans. I read an article by Mr. Nick Hills of Southam News Services in which he quoted one federal official as saying:
We thought at the time-1967-that it was pretty bureaucratic to make a qualified person go back home to pick up his visa, as the United States does. But we misjudged the number of people who

would want to take advantage of the new rule. We thought it would only be a few hundred.
The actual figures were far more than that: 26,000 in 1968, 42,000 in 1969 and 50,000 in 1970. The Sedgewick Report found that under the present system of appeal-if the present rate of appeals continues-the size of the staff of the Immigration Department and of the Immigration Appeal Board would need to be tripled, at least. This would, of course, represent an enormous cost increase. But apart from the question of cost, which I suppose we should bear if it were necessary in the name of justice, I suggest we are wrong here in principle and that we should alter our immigration laws except in exceptional cases, because surely the law ought always to be able to take care of the exception which can be justified on humanitarian principles.
But let the law follow the practice in other countries. Our immigration laws should not stray from the principle that Canada is our home. It is a home which, we hope, will always be friendly to visitors; we should not like to be thought of as an inhospitable nation any more than the average householder wishes to have the reputation of being inhospitable. But let us not be imposed upon. With all due consideration being given to humanitarianism, let us have laws which recognize that the rights of Canadian citizens extend far beyond any rights of citizens of nations abroad who find themselves in this country. I thank hon. members for their attention.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am almost overcome as I address you in this crowded, expectant, hushed House on this Friday afternoon. First, I wish to congratulate both the mover and the seconder of the Address. I think they acquitted themselves well; their performance was fine. I congratulate, too, those of my colleagues who preceded me in this very important debate.
Those who seek to analyse our parliamentary institution, and especially those who delight in criticizing it, do not in my view pay sufficient regard to the opportunity afforded by such debates as the debate on the Address. Here the Members of Parliament are in their representational character and, as I have said before in this House, representative government precedes even responsible government. It is tremendously important that members from the various parts of this country address themselves to the various needs, interests and challenges which face the nation. This is a most important part of our proceedings and I congratulate those who have gone before me on Mr. Speaker's list.
I note that many members have been referring to their constituencies. I shall not do this but I shall refer, rather, to the province from which I come, a province which embraces four constituencies. Next year Prince Edward Island celebrates the one-hundredth anniversary of its entry into confederation. Although our province was host to the meeting at which confederation was really decided upon in 1864 in Charlottetown, we remained aloof for a further six years. I hope many Members of Parliament will avail themselves of the opportunity to go to Prince Edward Island in 1973 because it will be a gala celebration. Indeed I have suggested to the leader of my party
February 25, 1972

that he hold there a meeting of the Dominion cabinet on the 1st day of July, 1973, which is the exact anniversary.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It would be April Fool's day.

On this occasion as we come to our centenary, we are naturally, in Prince Edward Island, taking stock of the events which have followed the decision of our forefathers in 1873. We are appraising and judging the treatment we have received as a member of the Canadian family. While we rejoice in our Canadian-ism, proud of the fact that the cradle of confederation is in our province, we do see at the present time some serious problems and we do look to Ottawa and feel there are many areas in which we have not been given the treatment we deserve.
In the first place, the unemployment statistics for Prince Edward Island, released in the latest batch of statistics, indicate a rate of something like 19 per cent. Just because we have had a high unemployment rate for so long is no reason that we should begin to like it-and we do not like it. I have sat here for four years and have listened to the former minister of finance indulge in prophecies that everything would be all right in short order, that we would go around a corner and lick inflation and lick unemployment. Whatever else that man will be, he will not be respected as much of a prophet. When I think of his performance in the field of prophecy, I hope he will never indulge in it in his new portfolio because any time I hear that man stand up and say there will be peace in our time, I will head for the bunkers or the high hills!
Another aspect is the failure of the government to do its part in its own administration in our province. As the months go by I have been watching the closing of federal offices or portions thereof in Charlottetown. We find that the citizens of Prince Edward Island, to carry on their dealings with the government of Canada-which serves them as it does other provinces-must negotiate with officials located outside Prince Edward Island. I maintain that every citizen of Prince Edward Island should be able to deal with the government of Canada and its departments in the province of Prince Edward Island.
I do not welcome the closing down of the unemployment insurance office and the moving of it to Moncton. I would not have welcomed it even had it worked, which it did not. I do not like the dismantling of the Post Office Department and the ever-degrading of the structure which remains on Prince Edward Island. This is a negative and an unhelpful step and is not what was intended when we entered Confederation in 1873. This gradual erosion threatens to make one of the provinces of Canada a branch plant of some regional group.
Nor do I like to see the federal government eluding and evading its specific constitutional responsibility in our particular province and for our people. I have watched as the development planners have moved to a stage whereby the federal government has sloughed off its responsibility for many of the fishing ports of Prince Edward Island which, according to section 91 of the British North America Act, do belong to Ottawa. We have the plan that only certain designated ports are to be maintained and the rest are to be forgotten. That lack of responsibility on the part
Speech from the Throne
of the federal government is not at all creditable. I watch the manoeuvring which goes on to designate the ports. I see that the port which is probably seen by most Canadians, the port of Covehead in the heart of the national park-a great fishing centre; even I catch all sorts of mackerel there in the summer-is on the undesignated list. That port is being denied the kind of service, maintenance and improvement which all fishing ports should get from the federal Department of Public Works.
I say, too, that there has been lack of concern about public works projects which would help our people. For years and years the federal government has been failing to bridge Rustico Bay, a little bay on the northern shore of Prince Edward Island. In a day and age when the Soviet Union and the United States can both get to the moon, surely to heavens the government of Canada can get across Rustico harbour as it planned to do. We built a highway through the national park to link it together, but they cannot get across that bay.
I also say that in many of its responsibilities the government is failing to move with sufficient dispatch. I think the world of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson). He is a great orator, a great Burns scholar, and for that alone I would have high regard for him; but the snail's pace which marks the building of a good airport in Charlottetown distresses and pains me and troubles the people of Prince Edward Island. Eastern Provincial Airways is giving us the finest service we have ever had. Planes are flying to Montreal with good capacity. The people appreciate the service and they use it, but you can only find 65 seats in the Charlottetown airport. You get 125 parking spaces, but only 65 seats. So unless everybody comes out with 2 cars, it seems to me the thing does not jibe.
We are also concerned that not sufficient progress is being planned for ferry needs at Cape Tormentine and Borden. We need these ships under way now, because with the way the tourists are flocking to Prince Edward Island-showing their good judgment and their good taste in doing so-we will need new ships, especially now that the government has repudiated its commitment to build the causeway. I say in an even more serious way that the development plan, which is the umbrella apparently under which the government at Ottawa has embraced all its dealings with Prince Edward Island, is not measuring up to the expectations of the people who voted for the provincial party which endorsed it a couple of years ago. The development plan is in fact accelerating those negative forces which are presently marring and hurting our economy.
Long before there was a development plan we had the drift away from the farm and the heavy pressures upon the small farmer and the small fisherman. It seems to me that after many years of planning, discussion and study the Prince Edward Island development plan is in itself accelerating those forces and movements which have been injuring and marring our economy for many years. We do not need that kind of accentuation of negative forces.
Also, we find to this day that with the manner in which the federal government sits on top of all the planning there are delays creeping in and needs which are not
294

February 25, 1972
Speech from the Throne
being met. From the latest issue of the Eastern Graphic, one of Prince Edward Island's finest newspapers, I read:
It has often been suggested in the past that Ottawa now dictates almost everything that happens in this province. A recent example of just how far Ottawa is prepared to go to see that its own people get the jobs in this province . . . with the appointment of a management consultant for the Charlottetown development program.
The article goes on to say that seven or more firms submitted bids to the provincial minister but Ottawa wanted someone else to get it. So for many months there was delay and argument and the project is not yet under way. I say-I have said this more than once, as have my colleagues-that we need far more action, far more consideration and far more assistance in the very important industry of agriculture, especially in reference to the potato industry.
There are many things that we Prince Edward Islanders reflect upon. We are too much wedded to our Canadian association ever to think of fulfilling our destiny in any other way. We are Canadians to the core, but we ask that although we are the smallest among the provinces we still be regarded as a province and that the rights which appertain thereto never be neglected or forgotten by the powerful governmental machinery here in Ottawa.
There is much in the Speech from the Throne if one were looking for literary satisfaction. The purple passages are appealing. Whatever else it lacks, it has plenty of mellifluous prose. I do not mind that; that does not upset me; smooth writing is all right.
But I was surprised at the amount of gall which entered the purple prose. I refer to the reference in the Throne Speech to isolationism. There is a tendency to attack isolationism here, there and everywhere. Considering what has been attempted by this government in the realm of foreign policy, I would have thought that they would not be the group which would immediately come out attacking isolationism.
The effort to dilute our role in NATO was one of the first gestures which this government made before the world. It was not one of the noblest ones. There have been many indications that it might be shuffling off some responsibilities which once we used to bear. I thought of the isolationism syndrome when I noted that we are going to have a permanent observer in Washington accredited to the Organization of American States. We will join the ranks of Spain, Israel and Guyana in that regard. This is not, in my opinion, a tremendously courageous move.
In the days of Sir Wilfrid Laurier discussions were held in Ottawa over Canada joining the Pan-American Union as it then was. In Mr. King's generation of leadership here, it was reflected upon, considered and studied, and in the governments which followed it was also thought about, reflected and considered. Now, if after 70 years we are actually going to appoint an observer I hardly believe that this is a courageous step.
Canada must play its part in the world. Of course, we could not adopt an isolationist role. It would not be our tradition. Our people, I believe, would not tolerate it. We had an inglorious period in the 1930s when that was the foolish role we did play. I hope that never again will we 
sink into that low mire of insensitivity, selfishness and inward-looking approach.
We must play our part, not as a super power but, I hope, as a great and decent country. Perhaps we have to realize from time to time that we do have limitations. I have often believed that we should sharpen up our external aid program. I never could believe that a country of our resources could have a meaningful program of aid to 67 countries in the world. I think we have to be more specific and selective. I have told this House that we may have some job in moving our priorities and I believe that our first priority should be the Commonwealth Caribbean, a place where because of our ties we could do something meaningful and useful for these neighbours of ours who should mean so much to us, whose political and economic institutions are so greatly challenged and whose viability is under threat every day of their existence.
I am ashamed today, as I was ashamed at the last Throne Speech, that the little country of Barbados can send to Ottawa three people to man a very efficient diplomatic mission while this country seemingly cannot- whether through austerity, obstinacy or lack of concern- open a mission in reciprocation in Bridgetown, Barbados. It is a disgrace.
Then, of course, there will be special problems to which we must apply ourselves as events move in the outer world, events which concern us and which will affect us greatly. We have been troubled in recent months over events on the other side of the world. My colleague, the vice-chairman of the External Affairs and National Defence Committee, mentioned yesterday the trip which he, I and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) made to India and Pakistan at a time of terrible travail for literally millions of people from East Pakistan.
We watched events and we came back with sorrowful hearts, and yet there was some satisfaction in that the people of Canada did take an interest in this. Of course, we did not do as much as we could or perhaps should have done, but Canadians from one end of the country to the other did assist and contribute in that terrible story of human suffering which went on in the refugee camps of Bengal.
Now, with a decisiveness which is unusual in events of this kind, we have a new situation and a new state, a new nation: the populous nation of Bangla Desh was created. But the problems that existed in what was East Pakistan and is now Bangla Desh are not at all over, and we have a great responsibility there. I think that the government was right in recognizing Bangla Desh; indeed, I called for recognition some time earlier. I did not want Canada to be entering a turtle race, to be the last one to do it. I do not like the idea that you merely detach someone who is accredited to a nearby country. I think that Bangla Desh deserves a separate mission and the thing to do is to send in a charge d'affaires immediately and then build your establishment on that.
I hope that we will welcome Bangla Desh into the Commonwealth, and I am troubled in this regard that the Commonwealth may not have been sufficiently used as an association and the machinery of that association in the problem which faced Bangla Desh in its creation. I do not believe that the Commonwealth machinery is useless.
February 25, 1972

It is a matter of profound regret that Pakistan thought it necessary to withdraw from the Commonwealth. There is no disposition on my part to see Pakistan cast into outer darkness and it would be to me a great satisfaction if that country should elect to return to the Commonwealth. I remember the many occasions in the five or six years in which I was honoured to serve at the General Assembly of the United Nations, when I recall the fine co-operation which existed on many matters between Pakistani delegates and Canadian delegates as we tried our best to cope with the multifarious and difficult problems which faced that universal body. But I believe we must turn our attention to Bangla Desh and I hope the government will move.
I think the minister was on the right track when he answered a question of mine yesterday. I hope we will move and try to inspire our people to believe that there is a great human problem there as that new country tries to pick itself up after terrible agony, and that the Commonwealth tie will really mean something and it will be not only government to government and state to state but people to people.
I notice a section in the Throne Speech referring to the seeking and strengthening of friendships with other nations both within and outside the councils and agencies of the United Nations. This, of course, refers to contacts with and visits to the leaders of the Soviet Union, Yugoslavia, and so on. I do not think there is anyone who would not agree with that sentiment. We would be foolish and myopic if we did not want to see everything possible done to diminish tensions, strengthen detente and broaden understanding among nations.
We do not however, and did not believe that it was the course of statesmanship or diplomacy for the Prime Minister of this country to use the soil of the Soviet Union for his gratuitous insults and improper utterances in regard to the United States, and in this I do not demur or defer from the earlier statements made by myself and my colleagues. We do not want to castigate our long-standing allies as we go about the work of improving relations with other countries.
As far I know, nobody in this House has taken notice of the visit of the President of the United States to the People's Republic of China. This strikes me as being one of the great events of this decade. While I am never bemused by the notion that summitry by itself, a face-to-face conference of leaders can unravel all the problems, I believe that tremendous good in the international field may flow from this visit.
I know it is glib and clever of the wiseacres of the press to describe it as a political gesture by the President of the
Speech from the Throne
United States, but I think they do him less than justice. He is not one of my favourite American presidents, but he is the man who has made this contact and, as he said himself, has broken down the walls which have existed for far too long. Perhaps, in that strange irony that is sometimes worked out in history, he with his point of view would be the logical man to break ground in this field.
In our own history, I have often thought of Sir Robert Borden, the great loyalist from Halifax, as the man who could most successfully put the British imperialists in their place when it was necessary. Perhaps it is a man like President Nixon who can, without great misunderstanding at home, clear away some of the unfortunate and unnecessary hindrances to dialogue between these two important countries.
I am very proud that my own leader visited China some months ago and conducted himself there as a statesman and made a great impression on his hosts and others.
Hear, hear!

We welcome this sort of development and I think we all should hope that the Nixon visit will bring about dividends for those who are trying to build up an equity of peace, understanding and good will.
There is just one more matter that I wish to deal with, Mr. Speaker. I began with a reference to the Prince Edward Island centennial and I shall close with a reference to the establishment of Heritage Canada. Naturally I approve of this, especially when it comes from a government which was deaf and uncaring to my pleas over several months to save the magnificent residence of Sir Robert Borden, "Glensmere". Nothing was done and it fell before the wrecker's crew and so a great piece of history disappeared. This government could not move, apparently, to set aside a holiday to commemorate Sir John A. Macdonald, the father of our country. Even at this late date we may see some preservation of our historic past and, if so, the government will find no more enthusiastic supporter than I to commend them-and I will even forget their past apostasy and former lack of concern.
Hear, hear!
Five o'clock.

Agreed.
